daughter on the coast-downs by Clevedon, “I shall take steps for
insuring my life for a thousand pounds.”

chapter_title:
CHAPTER I

THE FOLD AND THE SHEPHERD
text:
It was the outcome of a long and intimate conversation. Alice Madden,
aged nineteen, a plain, shy, gentle-mannered girl, short of stature,
and in movement something less than graceful, wore a pleased look as
she glanced at her father’s face and then turned her eyes across the
blue channel to the Welsh hills. She was flattered by the confidence
reposed in her, for Dr. Madden, reticent by nature, had never been
known to speak in the domestic circle about his pecuniary affairs. He
seemed to be the kind of man who would inspire his children with
affection: grave but benign, amiably diffident, with a hint of lurking
mirthfulness about his eyes and lips. And to-day he was in the best of
humours; professional prospects, as he had just explained to Alice,
were more encouraging than hitherto; for twenty years he had practised
medicine at Clevedon, but with such trifling emolument that the needs
of his large family left him scarce a margin over expenditure; now, at
the age of forty-nine—it was 1872—he looked forward with a larger
hope. Might he not reasonably count on ten or fifteen more years of
activity? Clevedon was growing in repute as a seaside resort; new
houses were rising; assuredly his practice would continue to extend.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rich characterization of Alice and Dr. Madden, revealing his idealism, financial struggles, and hopes for professional advancement that will be tragically cut short.
enrichment.best_quote: "for twenty years he had practised medicine at Clevedon, but with such trifling emolument that the needs of his large family left him scarce a margin over expenditure"
enrichment.summary: Alice is pleased by her father's confidence; we learn Dr. Madden has practiced medicine at Clevedon for twenty years with little income, but now sees improving prospects at age forty-nine.

context: This chunk immediately follows Dr. Madden's announcement to his daughter Alice that he will insure his life for a thousand pounds. It establishes the context for this decision: his improved financial prospects after twenty years of struggling as a country doctor in Clevedon, his optimistic expectations for further professional advancement, and his deepening relationship with his eldest daughter, whom he has begun to confide in about family matters usually kept private.

text:
“I don’t think girls ought to be troubled about this kind of thing,” he
added apologetically. “Let men grapple with the world; for, as the old
hymn says, “’tis their nature to.” I should grieve indeed if I thought
my girls would ever have to distress themselves about money matters.
But I find I have got into the habit, Alice, of talking to you very
much as I should talk with your dear mother if she were with us.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reveals Dr. Madden's paternalistic ideology about women and money, a key tension underlying the novel's central conflicts about female independence.
enrichment.best_quote: "Let men grapple with the world; for, as the old hymn says, 'tis their nature to."

He explains that while he doesn't believe girls should worry about financial matters, he has come to rely on Alice as a confidante regarding his pecuniary affairs, much as he would with her deceased mother. This reflects his protective but paternalistic views on women and money, as well as the family's financial precariousness despite his improving medical practice.

text:
Mrs. Madden, having given birth to six daughters, had fulfilled her
function in this wonderful world; for two years she had been resting in
the old churchyard that looks upon the Severn sea. Father and daughter
sighed as they recalled her memory. A sweet, calm, unpretending woman;
admirable in the domesticities; in speech and thought distinguished by
a native refinement, which in the most fastidious eyes would have
established her claim to the title of lady. She had known but little
repose, and secret anxieties told upon her countenance long before the
final collapse of health.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Provides necessary background about the deceased Mrs. Madden, though the passage is conventional elegiac prose.

“And yet,” pursued the doctor—doctor only by courtesy—when he had
stooped to pluck and examine a flower, “I made a point of never
discussing these matters with her. As no doubt you guess, life has been
rather an uphill journey with us. But the home must be guarded against
sordid cares to the last possible moment; nothing upsets me more than
the sight of those poor homes where wife and children are obliged to
talk from morning to night of how the sorry earnings shall be laid out.
No, no; women, old or young, should never have to think about money.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Deepens the characterization of Dr. Madden's idealism and reveals his deliberate sheltering of his family from financial realities—a strategy that will prove catastrophic.
enrichment.best_quote: "nothing upsets me more than the sight of those poor homes where wife and children are obliged to talk from morning to night of how the sorry earnings shall be laid out"
enrichment.summary: Dr. Madden explains that he deliberately kept financial worries from his wife, believing the home should be protected from sordid concerns.

context: Dr. Madden continues his conversation with his eldest daughter Alice during their walk, elaborating on his philosophy that women should be sheltered from financial worries. “There will come a day, Alice, when neither man nor woman is troubled
with such sordid care. Not yet awhile; no, no; but the day will come.
Human beings are not destined to struggle for ever like beasts of prey.
Give them time; let civilization grow. You know what our poet says:
“There the common sense of most shall hold a fretful realm in awe—””

He quoted the couplet with a subdued fervour which characterized the
man and explained his worldly lot. Elkanah Madden should never have
entered the medical profession; mere humanitarianism had prompted the
choice in his dreamy youth; he became an empiric, nothing more. “Our
poet,” said the doctor; Clevedon was chiefly interesting to him for its
literary associations. Tennyson he worshipped; he never passed
Coleridge’s cottage without bowing in spirit. From the contact of
coarse actualities his nature shrank.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brilliant characterization: the narrator explains why Dr. Madden's impractical idealism makes him unsuited to supporting his family, establishing the root cause of the novel's tragedy.
enrichment.best_quote: "Elkanah Madden should never have entered the medical profession; mere humanitarianism had prompted the choice in his dreamy youth; he became an empiric, nothing more."
enrichment.summary: The narrator reveals that Dr. Madden entered medicine from humanitarian idealism rather than aptitude, becoming merely a practitioner; he is more interested in literary associations than practical concerns.

context: Dr. Madden's romantic, literary nature and unsuitability for practical medicine. His idealistic temperament, devotion to poetry, and avoidance of harsh realities contribute to his financial struggles and inability to provide practical security for his family.

text:
When he and Alice returned from their walk it was the hour of family
tea. A guest was present this afternoon; the eight persons who sat down
to table were as many as the little parlour could comfortably contain.
Of the sisters, next in age to Alice came Virginia, a pretty but
delicate girl of seventeen. Gertrude, Martha, and Isabel, ranging from
fourteen to ten, had no physical charm but that of youthfulness; Isabel
surpassed her eldest sister in downright plainness of feature. The
youngest, Monica, was a bonny little maiden only just five years old,
dark and bright-eyed.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces the Madden daughters with efficient physical descriptions; establishes the scope of the family that will face hardship.
enrichment.summary: At family tea, eight persons sit at table including a guest; the daughters are described—Virginia is pretty and delicate, Gertrude, Martha, and Isabel are plain, and Monica is a bonny five-year-old.

The passage introduces all six of Dr. Madden's daughters by name and appearance, establishing the domestic scene at their home in Clevedon before the arrival of their guest, Rhoda Nunn, and before Dr. Madden receives an urgent call to attend a patient—an accident that will prove fatal.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER I

THE FOLD AND THE SHEPHERD
text:
The parents had omitted no care in shepherding their fold. Partly at
home, and partly in local schools, the young ladies had received
instruction suitable to their breeding, and the elder ones were
disposed to better this education by private study. The atmosphere of
the house was intellectual; books, especially the poets, lay in every
room. But it never occurred to Dr. Madden that his daughters would do
well to study with a professional object. In hours of melancholy he had
of course dreaded the risks of life, and resolved, always with
postponement, to make some practical provision for his family; in
educating them as well as circumstances allowed, he conceived that he
was doing the next best thing to saving money, for, if a fatality
befell, teaching would always be their resource. The thought, however,
of his girls having to work for money was so utterly repulsive to him
that he could never seriously dwell upon it. A vague piety supported
his courage. Providence would not deal harshly with him and his dear
ones. He enjoyed excellent health; his practice decidedly improved. The
one duty clearly before him was to set an example of righteous life,
and to develop the girls’ minds—in every proper direction. For, as to
training them for any path save those trodden by English ladies of the
familiar type, he could not have dreamt of any such thing. Dr. Madden’s
hopes for the race were inseparable from a maintenance of morals and
conventions such as the average man assumes in his estimate of women.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Crucial exposition: reveals the paradox at the heart of the novel—Dr. Madden educates his daughters to cultivate their minds while refusing to prepare them for independence, assuming Providence will protect them.
enrichment.best_quote: "In hours of melancholy he had of course dreaded the risks of life, and resolved, always with postponement, to make some practical provision for his family"
enrichment.summary: The Madden daughters receive an intellectual education suitable to their breeding, and Dr. Madden vaguely trusts that teaching could be their resource if necessary, but he is repulsed by the idea of them having to work and expects Providence to protect them.

context: This passage appears in paragraph 9 of the chapter. It follows Dr. Madden's return from his walk with Alice, where he has discussed his plan to insure his life and his optimistic views on the future. The chunk provides crucial exposition on Dr. Madden's approach to educating his six daughters—emphasizing his belief in intellectual development within conventional domestic roles, his reluctance to contemplate his daughters working for money despite recognizing teaching as a potential resource, and his faith in Providence rather than practical financial planning. This passage is significant as it establishes the family's precarious social position and foreshadows the tragedy to come, as Dr. Madden's accident and death will force his daughters to confront the very professional necessity he has refused to seriously consider.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER I

THE FOLD AND THE SHEPHERD
text:
The guest at table was a young girl named Rhoda Nunn. Tall, thin,
eager-looking, but with promise of bodily vigour, she was singled at a
glance as no member of the Madden family. Her immaturity (but fifteen,
she looked two years older) appeared in nervous restlessness, and in
her manner of speaking, childish at times in the hustling of
inconsequent thoughts, yet striving to imitate the talk of her seniors.
She had a good head, in both senses of the phrase; might or might not
develop a certain beauty, but would assuredly put forth the fruits of
intellect. Her mother, an invalid, was spending the summer months at
Clevedon, with Dr. Madden for medical adviser, and in this way the girl
became friendly with the Madden household. Its younger members she
treated rather condescendingly; childish things she had long ago put
away, and her sole pleasure was in intellectual talk. With a frankness
peculiar to her, indicative of pride, Miss Nunn let it be known that
she would have to earn her living, probably as a school teacher; study
for examinations occupied most of her day, and her hours of leisure
were frequently spent either at the Maddens or with a family named
Smithson—people, these latter, for whom she had a profound and
somewhat mysterious admiration. Mr. Smithson, a widower with a
consumptive daughter, was a harsh-featured, rough-voiced man of about
five-and-thirty, secretly much disliked by Dr. Madden because of his
aggressive radicalism; if women’s observation could be trusted, Rhoda
Nunn had simply fallen in love with him, had made him, perhaps
unconsciously, the object of her earliest passion. Alice and Virginia
commented on the fact in their private colloquy with a shamefaced
amusement; they feared that it spoke ill for the young lady’s breeding.
None the less they thought Rhoda a remarkable person, and listened to
her utterances respectfully.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces Rhoda Nunn with striking characterization: ambitious, intellectually serious, and dangerously idealistic about earning her own living and attracted to radical ideas—contrasts sharply with the sheltered Madden daughters.
enrichment.best_quote: "With a frankness peculiar to her, indicative of pride, Miss Nunn let it be known that she would have to earn her living, probably as a school teacher"
enrichment.summary: Rhoda Nunn, a fifteen-year-old guest, is described as tall, intellectual, and destined to earn her living as a teacher; she harbors an unrequited passion for the radical widower Mr. Smithson.

context: This passage introduces Rhoda Nunn, a fifteen-year-old guest at the Maddens' tea table. It establishes her character as an intellectually precocious girl determined to earn her living as a teacher, contrasting sharply with Dr. Madden's conventional views on women's roles. The passage also reveals her infatuation with Mr. Smithson, a radical widower, which concerns the Madden sisters about her propriety while simultaneously impressing them with her independent spirit.

It was always thus. Dr. Madden did not care to discuss even playfully
the radical notions which Rhoda got from her objectionable friend. His
daughters would not have ventured to express an opinion on such topics
when he was present; apart with Miss Nunn, they betrayed a timid
interest in whatever proposition she advanced, but no gleam of
originality distinguished their arguments.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reveals Dr. Madden's refusal to engage with radical ideas and his daughters' intellectual timidity—they are unprepared for independent thought, central to the novel's tragedy.

context: This passage describes Dr. Madden's dismissive attitude toward progressive political ideas, particularly those influenced by the radical Mr. Smithson. The chunk reveals the tension between the doctor's Victorian conservatism and the younger generation's emerging intellectual independence.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER I

THE FOLD AND THE SHEPHERD
text:
After tea the little company fell into groups—some out of doors
beneath the apple-trees, others near the piano at which Virginia was
playing Mendelssohn. Monica ran about among them with her five-year-old
prattle, ever watched by her father, who lounged in a canvas chair
against the sunny ivied wall, pipe in mouth. Dr. Madden was thinking
how happy they made him, these kind, gentle girls; how his love for
them seemed to ripen with every summer; what a delightful old age his
would be, when some were married and had children of their own, and the
others tended him—they whom he had tended. Virginia would probably be
sought in marriage; she had good looks, a graceful demeanour, a bright
understanding. Gertrude also, perhaps. And little Monica—ah, little
Monica! she would be the beauty of the family. When Monica had grown up
it would be time for him to retire from practice; by then he would
doubtless have saved money.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Poignant glimpse of Dr. Madden's paternal contentment and dreams for his daughters' futures—tragically soon to be disrupted.
enrichment.best_quote: "How happy they made him, these kind, gentle girls; how his love for them seemed to ripen with every summer; what a delightful old age his would be, when some were married and had children of their own, and the others tended him—they whom he had tended."
enrichment.summary: Dr. Madden contentedly watches his daughters; he dreams of some marrying and others caring for him in his old age, expecting he will have saved money by the time Monica reaches adulthood.

context: Dr. Madden relaxes at home after tea with his daughters and guest Rhoda Nunn, contentedly contemplating his children's futures and his own retirement, unaware of the fatal accident that will soon befall him.

preference. Little persuasion was needed. Alice brought the volume, and
he selected “The Lotus-Eaters.” The girls grouped themselves about him,
delighted to listen. Many an hour of summer evening had they thus
spent, none more peaceful than the present. The reader’s cadenced voice
blended with the song of a thrush.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER I

THE FOLD AND THE SHEPHERD
text:
By nine o’clock the younger trio of sisters had gone to bed; Alice,
Virginia, and Gertrude sat in the parlour, occupied with books, from
time to time exchanging a quiet remark. A tap at the door scarcely drew
their attention, for they supposed it was the maid-servant coming to
lay supper. But when the door opened there was a mysterious silence;
Alice looked up and saw the expected face, wearing, however, so strange
an expression that she rose with sudden fear.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Builds suspenseful atmosphere and introduces the event that will reshape the entire narrative—Alice's sudden fear at the maid's expression signals impending tragedy.
enrichment.best_quote: "A tap at the door scarcely drew their attention, for they supposed it was the maid-servant coming to lay supper."
enrichment.summary: Late evening, the three eldest sisters are reading quietly when the maid enters with a mysterious expression that alarms Alice.

context: Dr. Madden has just been called away on an emergency house call to treat a farmer. While his daughters await his return, a servant arrives at the parlor door with urgent news: Dr. Madden has been thrown from his horse and lies insensible at a roadside cottage. This moment marks the turning point where the family's secure, comfortable life is about to be shattered by tragedy.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER I

THE FOLD AND THE SHEPHERD
text:
For some time the doctor had been intending to buy a new horse; his
faithful old roadster was very weak in the knees. As in other matters,
so in this, postponement became fatality; the horse stumbled and fell,
and its driver was flung head forward into the road. Some hours later
they brought him to his home, and for a day or two there were hopes
that he might rally. But the sufferer’s respite only permitted him to
dictate and sign a brief will; this duty performed, Dr. Madden closed
his lips for ever.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The doctor's death is narrated with grim economy: his postponement of buying a new horse—a minor prudential failure—becomes fatal. This poignant irony crystallizes the novel's core tragedy.
enrichment.best_quote: "As in other matters, so in this, postponement became fatality; the horse stumbled and fell, and its driver was flung head forward into the road."
enrichment.summary: Dr. Madden's old horse, which he had long postponed replacing, stumbles and throws him; after a brief hope for recovery, he dies, having only had time to dictate a brief will.

context: Dr. Madden is called away from reading poetry to his daughters to attend to a medical emergency. While driving back from Kingston Seymour in his old, weakened horse-drawn cart, he is thrown from his vehicle and fatally injured. This accident, caused by his characteristic postponement of practical matters, results in his death and leaves his family—particularly his six daughters—without the financial provision he had only just begun to consider.

text:
Having allowed exactly a week to go by, Everard Barfoot made use of his
cousin’s permission, and called upon her at nine in the evening. Miss
Barfoot’s dinner-hour was seven o’clock; she and Rhoda, when alone,
rarely sat for more than half an hour at table, and in this summer
season they often went out together at sunset to enjoy a walk along the
river. This evening they had returned only a few minutes before
Everard’s ring sounded at the door. Miss Barfoot (they were just
entering the library) looked at her friend and smiled.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine scene-setting establishing the time and place of Everard's visit.
enrichment.summary: Everard Barfoot calls on his cousin Mary Barfoot and Rhoda Nunn in the evening, arriving shortly after they have returned from a walk.

context: This chunk opens a chapter depicting Everard Barfoot's second visit to his cousin Miss Barfoot's home, where he will engage Rhoda Nunn in intellectual debate about women's education, marriage, and social reform. The passage establishes the domestic setting and timing of the evening visit.

text:
“I shouldn’t wonder if that is the young man. Very flattering if he has
come again so soon.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Minor commentary by Mary Barfoot, conversational and unremarkable.
enrichment.summary: Mary Barfoot speculates pleasantly that the visitor is Everard and remarks on his prompt return.

context: Miss Barfoot's reaction upon hearing Everard Barfoot's arrival at her home, commenting to Rhoda Nunn that her cousin has returned to visit them only a week after his previous visit, which she finds flattering.

text:
The visitor was in mirthful humour, and met with a reception of
corresponding tone. He remarked at once that Miss Nunn had a much
pleasanter aspect than a week ago; her smile was ready and agreeable;
she sat in a sociable attitude and answered a jesting triviality with
indulgence.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes Everard's tone and Rhoda's improved demeanor, preparing for substantive dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Everard arrives in good humor and is met with a warm reception; Rhoda appears more pleasant and sociable than at their first meeting.

context: Everard Barfoot's second visit to his cousin Miss Barfoot's house, where he finds Miss Rhoda Nunn in improved spirits and more receptive demeanor than during his first visit a week prior.

text:
“One of my reasons for coming to-day,” said Everard, “was to tell you a
remarkable story. It connects”—he addressed his cousin—“with our talk
about the matrimonial disasters of those two friends of mine. Do you
remember the name of Micklethwaite—a man who used to cram me with
mathematics? I thought you would. He is on the point of marrying, and
his engagement has lasted just seventeen years.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces the Micklethwaite story as a device to discuss marriage and engagement, moderately relevant to themes.
enrichment.summary: Everard announces he has a remarkable story about his friend Micklethwaite, who has been engaged for seventeen years.

context: Everard Barfoot visits his cousin Miss Barfoot and her friend Rhoda Nunn a week after their first meeting. Upon arrival, he is in good humor and finds Rhoda in a pleasant mood. He begins to tell them about an acquaintance, Micklethwaite, a mathematics tutor from his youth, who is about to marry after a seventeen-year engagement, using this story as a springboard for discussing poverty's role in delayed marriages and launching into broader philosophical debates about marriage, women's education, and gender relations that will dominate the evening's conversation.

text: “The wisest of your friends, I should say.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief, conventional response by Mary Barfoot.
enrichment.summary: Mary Barfoot judges Micklethwaite to be the wisest of Everard's friends.

context: This is Miss Barfoot's response to Everard's story about his friend Micklethwaite, who has been engaged for seventeen years and is finally about to marry. She is praising the wisdom of a long engagement, suggesting that prolonged courtship before marriage is prudent.

text:
“An excellent fellow. He is forty, and the lady the same. An
astonishing case of constancy.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine exposition about Micklethwaite's age and engagement duration.
enrichment.summary: Everard describes Micklethwaite as an excellent fellow of forty, engaged for seventeen years.

context: Everard is describing his friend Micklethwaite, who has been engaged for seventeen years and is finally about to marry. Both he and his fiancée are forty years old, and their long engagement was due to poverty rather than lack of commitment.

text: “And how is it likely to turn out?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Simple question advancing the Micklethwaite anecdote.
enrichment.summary: Mary Barfoot asks how the marriage is likely to turn out.

context: Everard tells Miss Barfoot and Rhoda Nunn about his friend Micklethwaite's seventeen-year engagement. When Miss Barfoot asks this question, she is inquiring about the prospects for Micklethwaite's impending marriage to his long-time fiancée.

text:
“I can’t predict, as the lady is unknown to me. But,” he added with
facetious gravity, “I think it likely that they are tolerably well
acquainted with each other. Nothing but sheer poverty has kept them
apart. Pathetic, don’t you think? I have a theory that when an
engagement has lasted ten years, with constancy on both sides, and
poverty still prevents marriage, the State ought to make provision for
a man in some way, according to his social standing. When one thinks of
it, a whole socialistic system lies in that suggestion.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard proposes a socialistic theory linking long engagements, poverty, and state provision, opening thematic discussion of marriage and social reform.
enrichment.best_quote: I have a theory that when an engagement has lasted ten years, with constancy on both sides, and poverty still prevents marriage, the State ought to make provision for a man in some way, according to his social standing. When one thinks of it, a whole socialistic system lies in that suggestion.
enrichment.summary: Everard theorizes that the State should provide for couples whose long engagements are prevented only by poverty, sketching a satirical socialistic system.

context: Everard Barfoot recounts the remarkable story of his former tutor Micklethwaite, who has been engaged for seventeen years to a woman of the same age. Unable to marry due to poverty despite their constancy, Barfoot uses this case to propose a provocative theory: the State should provide financial support to men in such circumstances, suggesting an entire socialistic system could be built on this idea.

text:
“If,” remarked Rhoda, “it were first provided that no marriage should
take place until  after  a ten years’ engagement.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's sharp, witty addition to Everard's proposal, revealing her sharp intellect and satirical approach to social reform.
enrichment.best_quote: If it were first provided that no marriage should take place until after a ten years' engagement.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda completes Everard's system by proposing that no marriage occur before a ten-year engagement period.

context: Rhoda responds to Everard's proposal for state provision to couples engaged for ten years by suggesting that no marriage should be permitted until after a ten-year engagement period has elapsed—a satirical extension of his socialistic theory about matrimonial reform.

text:
“Yes,” Barfoot assented, in his smoothest and most graceful tone. “That
completes the system. Unless you like to add that no engagement is
permitted except between people who have passed a certain examination;
equivalent, let us say, to that which confers a university degree.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard extends the satire with an examination requirement, deepening the intellectual sparring about marriage and social standards.
enrichment.best_quote: That completes the system. Unless you like to add that no engagement is permitted except between people who have passed a certain examination; equivalent, let us say, to that which confers a university degree.
enrichment.summary: Everard adds an educational requirement to the satirical system, proposing only those with university-equivalent education be permitted to engage.

context: Everard Barfoot is engaged in a debate with Rhoda Nunn and his cousin Mary Barfoot about marriage, women's education, and social reform. Rhoda has proposed that no marriage should take place until after a ten-year engagement. Everard responds by sarcastically extending her proposal, suggesting that engagements should only be permitted between people who have passed a university-level examination, further developing the discussion about ideal conditions for matrimony.

text:
“Admirable. And no marriage, except where both, for the whole
decennium, have earned their living by work that the State recognizes.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda pushes the satire further by adding an economic requirement, demonstrating her ideological commitment to work and independence.
enrichment.best_quote: And no marriage, except where both, for the whole decennium, have earned their living by work that the State recognizes.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda adds that both parties must have earned their living through State-recognized work for the entire engagement period.

context: This chunk is part of a debate between Everard Barfoot and Rhoda Nunn about marriage and women's education. Rhoda proposes that marriage should only be permitted after a ten-year engagement during which both partners have earned their living through state-recognized work. The conversation occurs early in Everard's first visit to Miss Barfoot's house, where he has come to discuss his friend Micklethwaite's long engagement and broader ideas about reforming marriage and women's roles in society.

text:
“How would that affect Mr. Micklethwaite’s betrothed?” asked Miss
Barfoot.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Practical question about Micklethwaite's fiancée's work status.
enrichment.summary: Mary Barfoot asks whether Micklethwaite's fiancée meets the proposed economic requirements.

context: Miss Barfoot asks this question during a discussion about Everard's proposed "socialistic system" for marriages with long engagements, where both parties must have passed examinations and earned their living through state-recognized work for ten years. Rhoda has just outlined her additions to this system, and Miss Barfoot seeks clarification about how these strict requirements would apply to Mr. Micklethwaite, a man Everard mentioned whose engagement has lasted seventeen years due to poverty.

text: “I believe she has supported herself all along by teaching.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief factual response about the fiancée's occupation.
enrichment.summary: Everard reveals that Micklethwaite's fiancée has supported herself by teaching.

context: Everard discusses the long engagement of his friend Micklethwaite and asks about his fiancée's occupation, to which Rhoda replies that she has supported herself through teaching, leading to a broader debate about women's work and independence.

text:
“Of course!” exclaimed the other impatiently. “And more likely than
not, with loathing of her occupation. The usual kind of drudgery, was
it?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mary Barfoot's sharp critique of women teachers and their exploitation, establishing her ideological stance on women's work.
enrichment.best_quote: And more likely than not, with loathing of her occupation. The usual kind of drudgery, was it?
enrichment.summary: Mary Barfoot expresses frustration that the fiancée has likely endured years of uncongenial drudgery as a teacher.

context: Miss Barfoot responds impatiently to Everard's mention that Mr. Micklethwaite's betrothed has supported herself by teaching, expressing her disdain for the typical female teacher who performs tedious work while longing for marriage as an escape from her drudgery.

text: “After all, there must be some one to teach children to read and write.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard offers a mild counterpoint, but the response is routine.
enrichment.summary: Everard notes that someone must teach children, a necessary function.

context: This quote occurs during a debate between Everard Barfoot and Rhoda Nunn about women's education and employment. Rhoda has criticized the "usual kind of drudgery" of teaching, arguing that women should be trained for diverse professions rather than defaulting to teaching. Everard responds with this pragmatic counterpoint, noting the practical necessity of the profession, which Rhoda then dismisses as inadequate justification for perpetuating women's limited occupational choices.

text:
“Yes; but people who are thoroughly well trained for the task, and who
take a pleasure in it. This lady may be an exception; but I picture her
as having spent a lifetime of uncongenial toil, longing miserably for
the day when poor Mr. Micklethwaite was able to offer her a home.
That’s the ordinary teacher-woman, and we must abolish her altogether.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mary Barfoot's passionate articulation of women's right to professional training and meaningful work, a core thematic statement on feminism and women's independence.
enrichment.best_quote: But girls are to be brought up to a calling in life, just as men are. It's because they have no calling that, when need comes, they all offer themselves as teachers.
enrichment.summary: Mary Barfoot argues that women must be trained to professions with the same care as men, and that teaching is a desperate fallback precisely because women lack real vocational options.

context: This chunk is part of a debate between Rhoda Nunn and Everard Barfoot about women's education and employment. Rhoda argues that women should be trained for definite professions rather than defaulting to teaching as an occupation of last resort. She criticizes the "ordinary teacher-woman" who takes up teaching only out of financial necessity and with distaste for the work, using Mr. Micklethwaite's long-suffering fiancée (a teacher) as an example of this type of woman who must work in uncongenial toil while waiting for marriage to provide her with a home.

text:
“How are you to do that?” inquired Everard suavely. “The average man
labours that he may be able to marry, and the average woman certainly
has the same end in view. Are female teachers to be vowed to celibacy?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard raises a practical objection about women's dual responsibility to work and marriage, touching on a real tension.
enrichment.summary: Everard notes that women cannot pursue lifelong careers if marriage is a likely outcome, unlike men.

context: Everard challenges Rhoda's argument that women should pursue professions and callings like men do. He questions how she would prevent women from defaulting to teaching as their only career option while still allowing them to marry, suggesting her system would effectively force female teachers into celibacy.

text:
“Nothing of the kind. But girls are to be brought up to a calling in
life, just as men are. It’s because they have no calling that, when
need comes, they all offer themselves as teachers. They undertake one
of the most difficult and arduous pursuits as if it were as simple as
washing up dishes. We can’t earn money in any other way, but we can
teach children! A man only becomes a schoolmaster or tutor when he has
gone through laborious preparation—anything but wise or adequate, of
course, but still conscious preparation; and only a very few men,
comparatively, choose that line of work. Women must have just as wide a
choice.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mary Barfoot's powerful rebuttal that professional training transforms women into complete human beings with equality, articulating the novel's core feminist argument.
enrichment.best_quote: No. Not henceforth profitless! There's the very point I insist upon. So far is it from profitless, that it has made her a wholly different woman from what she would otherwise have been. Instead of a moping, mawkish creature, with—in most instances—a very unhealthy mind, she is a complete human being. She stands on an equality with the man.
enrichment.summary: Mary Barfoot argues that professional training, even if abandoned for marriage, fundamentally improves women's character and enables equality with men.

context: This passage is part of a debate between Rhoda Nunn and Everard Barfoot about women's education and professional opportunities. Rhoda argues that girls should receive proper vocational training like boys do, rather than defaulting to teaching as their only option when they need to earn money. She criticizes how women undertake teaching without adequate preparation, while men receive rigorous training for the same profession. Rhoda advocates for women to have the same breadth of career choices as men.

text:
“That’s plausible, cousin Mary. But remember that when a man chooses
his calling he chooses it for life. A girl cannot but remember that if
she marries her calling at once changes. The old business is thrown
aside—henceforth profitless.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard concedes gracefully and raises a practical question about women with domestic obligations.
enrichment.summary: Everard acknowledges Mary's view and asks how unmarried women constrained by family duties should be treated.

context: Everard argues that women choosing professions face a different situation than men because marriage would cause them to abandon their careers, making their professional training ultimately pointless—a point Rhoda contests by asserting that professional work fundamentally improves a woman's character and equality with men, regardless of whether she later marries.

text:
“No. Not henceforth profitless! There’s the very point I insist upon.
So far is it from profitless, that it has made her a wholly different
woman from what she would otherwise have been. Instead of a moping,
mawkish creature, with—in most instances—a very unhealthy mind, she
is a complete human being. She stands on an equality with the man. He
can’t despise her as he now does.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mary Barfoot's comprehensive vision for female education and duty, rejecting idleness and middle-class vulgarization, synthesizing key feminist and social reform arguments.
enrichment.best_quote: And when the whole course of female education is altered; when girls are trained as a matter of course to some definite pursuit; then those who really are obliged to remain at home will do their duty there in quite a different spirit.
enrichment.summary: Mary Barfoot proposes universal professional training for all girls, ensuring that domestic duties become conscious choice rather than idle drudgery.

context: Rhoda Nunn argues that women's professional work, even if abandoned after marriage, fundamentally transforms them into complete human beings capable of standing as equals to men, rather than remaining the dependent, unhealthy creatures society currently produces. She insists this is not profitless but essential to preventing male contempt in marriage.

text:
“Very good,” assented Everard, observing Miss Nunn’s satisfied smile.
“I like that view very much. But what about the great number of girls
who are claimed by domestic duties? Do you abandon them, with a
helpless sigh, to be moping and mawkish and unhealthy?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard makes a supportive interjection, but it is routine.
enrichment.summary: Everard agrees that men too should not be idle and vulgarized.

context: Everard questions Rhoda's proposal that all girls should be trained in a profession, asking what should happen to girls obligated to domestic duties at home. This occurs during a debate between Everard and Rhoda about female education, independence, and marriage, where Rhoda argues that women should have professional callings like men to avoid becoming mentally unhealthy dependents.

text:
“In the first place, there needn’t be a great number of unmarried women
claimed by such duties. Most of those you are thinking of are not
fulfilling a duty at all; they are only pottering about the house,
because they have nothing better to do. And when the whole course of
female education is altered; when girls are trained as a matter of
course to some definite pursuit; then those who really are obliged to
remain at home will do their duty there in quite a different spirit.
Home work will be their serious business, instead of a disagreeable
drudgery, or a way of getting through the time till marriage offers. I
would have no girl, however wealthy her parent, grow up without a
profession. There should be no such thing as a class of females
vulgarized by the necessity of finding daily amusement.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's brief affirmation is conversational filler.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda agrees with Everard's extension of the principle to men.

context: This passage is Rhoda Nunn's response to Everard Barfoot's question about unmarried women claimed by domestic duties. She argues for comprehensive female education and professional training, asserting that all girls should develop a definite calling to avoid idleness and moral degradation, whether they marry or remain single. This is part of a broader debate between Rhoda and Everard about women's independence, marriage, and self-respect that dominates their conversation during his second visit to Miss Barfoot's house.

text: “Nor of males either, of course,” put in Everard, stroking his beard.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard tests Rhoda's orthodoxy by asking if she endorses the most extreme position—that marriage should be discouraged entirely.
enrichment.summary: Everard asks whether Rhoda fully supports the radical position articulated in the discussion.

context: Everard is responding to Rhoda's argument that girls should be trained to professions rather than left idle at home, agreeing that idle males shouldn't exist either. This is part of a broader debate about female education and independence where Rhoda advocates for women to have careers and self-respect before marriage.

text: “Nor of males either, cousin Everard.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's declaration that marriage should be taught as a disgrace to be avoided, revealing her uncompromising radical position and central to understanding her character.
enrichment.best_quote: Oh yes. But I go further. I would have girls taught that marriage is a thing to be avoided rather than hoped for. I would teach them that for the majority of women marriage means disgrace.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda declares that she would teach girls to regard marriage as shameful and to be avoided, revealing her radical feminist stance.

context: Rhoda Nunn agrees with Miss Barfoot's argument that all girls should be trained to a profession, adding her own conviction that no one—regardless of gender—should grow up without purposeful work to avoid becoming idle and vulgar. When Everard acknowledges this principle applies to males too, Rhoda firmly concurs with his statement.

text: “You thoroughly approve all this, Miss Nunn?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard probes Rhoda's reasoning, seeking to understand her extreme position.
enrichment.summary: Everard asks Rhoda to clarify why she considers marriage a disgrace.

context: In a discussion about women's education and financial independence, Miss Barfoot asks Rhoda Nunn if she approves of the idea that girls should be trained for a profession or calling in life, rather than viewing marriage as their primary purpose.

text:
“Oh yes. But I go further. I would have girls taught that marriage is a
thing to be avoided rather than hoped for. I would teach them that for
the majority of women marriage means disgrace.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's stark pronouncement that men lack honor and marriage means bondage to dishonorable men, articulating her contempt for men and rationale for anti-marriage ideology.
enrichment.best_quote: Because the majority of men are without sense of honour. To be bound to them in wedlock is shame and misery.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda declares that most men lack honor and that marriage to them is shameful and miserable for women.

context: Rhoda Nunn expresses her radical views on marriage and women's independence during a dinner conversation at Miss Barfoot's house. When asked if she approves of the discussion about female education and professional training, she goes further than Miss Barfoot's moderate position, advocating that women should be taught to avoid marriage altogether because she believes it represents disgrace for most women due to men's lack of honor.

text: “Ah! Now do let me understand you. Why does it mean disgrace?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's reaction beats, brief and transitional.
enrichment.summary: Everard pauses, appearing troubled by Rhoda's vehement statement.

context: Everard questions Rhoda about her claim that marriage means disgrace for most women, pushing her to explain her radical views on matrimony and female independence during a discussion about women's education and self-respect.

text:
“Because the majority of men are without sense of honour. To be bound
to them in wedlock is shame and misery.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard challenges Rhoda's logic by questioning whether discouraging marriage will reform men's morality.
enrichment.summary: Everard asks whether Rhoda truly believes that persuading women to avoid marriage will improve men's character.

context: Rhoda Nunn's response when Everard Barfoot asks her to explain why she believes marriage means disgrace for most women, as part of their debate about women's independence, education, and the moral failings of men in matrimonial relationships.

text: Everard’s eyelids drooped, and he did not speak for a moment.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's articulate response reframing her mission as liberation of living women and long-term transformation of society through universal female self-respect, the ideological heart of her character.
enrichment.best_quote: I have no hope of sudden results, Mr. Barfoot. I should like to save as many as possible of the women now living from a life of dishonour; but the spirit of our work looks to the future. When all women, high and low alike, are trained to self-respect, then men will regard them in a different light, and marriage may be honourable to both.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda clarifies that her immediate goal is to protect living women from harmful marriages, while her ultimate vision is a future where universal female education and self-respect transforms the possibility of honorable marriage.

context: Everard is momentarily silent and thoughtful after Rhoda expresses her extreme view that marriage means disgrace for most women because most men lack honor. His silence suggests he is processing the radical nature of her statement before responding.

text:
“And you seriously think, Miss Nunn, that by persuading as many women
as possible to abstain from marriage you will improve the character of
men?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's silent reaction after Rhoda's passionate declaration.
enrichment.summary: Everard falls silent, apparently impressed by Rhoda's statement.

context: Everard Barfoot is challenging Rhoda Nunn's radical feminist position that marriage is dishonorable for women. Rhoda has just argued that women should be taught to avoid marriage because most men lack moral integrity. Everard questions whether her strategy of encouraging female celibacy will actually reform male behavior.

text:
“I have no hope of sudden results, Mr. Barfoot. I should like to save
as many as possible of the women now living from a life of dishonour;
but the spirit of our work looks to the future. When  all  women, high
and low alike, are trained to self-respect, then men will regard them
in a different light, and marriage may be honourable to both.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mary Barfoot's pragmatic interruption to change the subject.

Rhoda led him to the drawing-room, excused herself for a few moments,
and came back in her ordinary evening dress. Barfoot noticed that her
hair was much more becomingly arranged than when he first saw her; so
it had been on the last occasion, but for some reason its appearance
attracted his eyes this evening. He scrutinized her, at discreet
intervals, from head to foot. To Everard, nothing female was alien;
woman, merely as woman, interested him profoundly. And this example of
her sex had excited his curiosity in no common degree. His concern with
her was purely intellectual; she had no sensual attraction for him, but
he longed to see further into her mind, to probe the sincerity of the
motives she professed, to understand her mechanism, her process of
growth. Hitherto he had enjoyed no opportunity of studying this type.
For his cousin was a very different person; by habit he regarded her as
old, whereas Miss Nunn, in spite of her thirty years, could not
possibly be considered past youth.

He enjoyed her air of equality; she sat down with him as a male
acquaintance might have done, and he felt sure that her behaviour would
be the same under any circumstances. He delighted in the frankness of
her speech; it was doubtful whether she regarded any subject as
improper for discussion between mature and serious people. Part cause
of this, perhaps, was her calm consciousness that she had not a
beautiful face. No, it was not beautiful; yet even at the first meeting
it did not repel him. Studying her features, he saw how fine was their
expression. The prominent forehead, with its little unevenness that
meant brains; the straight eyebrows, strongly marked, with deep
vertical furrows generally drawn between them; the chestnut-brown eyes,
with long lashes; the high-bridged nose, thin and delicate; the
intellectual lips, a protrusion of the lower one, though very slight,
marking itself when he caught her profile; the big, strong chin; the
shapely neck—why, after all, it was a kind of beauty. The head might
have been sculptured with fine effect. And she had a well-built frame.
He observed her strong wrists, with exquisite vein-tracings on the pure
white. Probably her constitution was very sound; she had good teeth,
and a healthy brownish complexion.

go without rational training? Of course I know that Monica was only a

Luxurious fashion, as might have been expected, distinguished Mrs.
Luke’s drawing-room. Costly and beautiful things superabounded; perfume
soothed the air. Only since her bereavement had Mrs. Widdowson been
able to indulge this taste for modern exuberance in domestic adornment.
The deceased Luke was a plain man of business, who clung to the
fashions which had been familiar to him in his youth; his second wife
found a suburban house already furnished, and her influence with him
could not prevail to banish the horrors amid which he chose to live:
chairs in maroon rep, Brussels carpets of red roses on a green ground,
horse-hair sofas of the most uncomfortable shape ever designed,
antimacassars everywhere, chimney ornaments of cut glass trembling in
sympathy with the kindred chandeliers. She belonged to an obscure
branch of a house that culminated in an obscure baronetcy; penniless
and ambitious, she had to thank her imposing physique for rescue at a
perilous age, and though despising Mr. Luke Widdowson for his plebeian
tastes, she shrewdly retained the good-will of a husband who seemed no
candidate for length of years. The money-maker died much sooner than
she could reasonably have hoped, and left her an income of four
thousand pounds. Thereupon began for Mrs. Luke a life of feverish
aspiration. The baronetcy to which she was akin had inspired her, even
from childhood, with an aristocratic ideal; a handsome widow of only
eight-and-thirty, she resolved that her wealth should pave the way for
her to a titled alliance. Her acquaintance lay among City people, but
with the opportunities of freedom it was soon extended to the sphere of
what is known as smart society; her flat in Victoria Street attracted a
heterogeneous cluster of pleasure-seekers and fortune-hunters, among
them one or two vagrant members of the younger aristocracy. She lived
at the utmost pace compatible with technical virtue. When, as shortly
happened, it became evident that her income was not large enough for
her serious purpose, she took counsel with an old friend great in
finance, and thenceforth the excitement of the gambler gave a new zest
to her turbid existence. Like most of her female associates, she had
free recourse to the bottle; but for such stimulus the life of a smart
woman would be physically impossible. And Mrs. Luke enjoyed life,
enjoyed it vastly. The goal of her ambition, if all went well in the
City, was quite within reasonable hope. She foretasted the day when a
vulgar prefix would no longer attach to her name, and when the journals
of society would reflect her rising effulgence.

It was with no little curiosity that, on the appointed morning, Barfoot
repaired to South Tottenham. He had seen a photograph of Miss Wheatley,
but it dated from seventeen years ago. Standing in her presence, he was
moved with compassion, and with another feeling more rarely excited in
him by a woman’s face, that of reverential tenderness. Impossible to
recognize in this countenance the features known to him from the
portrait. At three-and-twenty she had possessed a sweet, simple
comeliness on which any man’s eye would have rested with pleasure; at
forty she was wrinkled, hollow-cheeked, sallow, indelible weariness
stamped upon her brow and lips. She looked much older than Mary
Barfoot, though they were just of an age. And all this for want of a
little money. The life of a pure, gentle, tender-hearted woman worn
away in hopeless longing and in hard struggle for daily bread. As she
took his hand and thanked him with an exquisite modesty for the present
she had received, Everard felt a lump rise in his throat. He was
ashamed to notice that the years had dealt so unkindly with her; fixing
his look upon her eyes, he gladdened at the gladness which shone in
them, at the soft light which they could still shed forth.

Everard is moved to tears by her modesty and the tragedy of her sacrificed life, yet her eyes still shine with gladness and tenderness.

appearance. He had seen her from time to time, and always with the love

standing before the glass to mark and comment upon his own. It was
enough to glance at him as he took his place beside her, the proudest
and happiest of men. A miracle had been wrought for him; kind fate, in

# Context: Everard's Reflections on Proposing to Rhoda

After his encounter with Rhoda Nunn in Chelsea Hospital gardens, Everard Barfoot returns home in a state of fascination with her strong-minded character. Reflecting on their conversation and her physical presence, he contemplates the possibility of deepening their relationship. This passage captures his consideration of marriage as a way to secure her companionship, while simultaneously questioning whether a conventional proposal would be appropriate given her independent nature and modern views. He entertains the unconventional alternative of suggesting a free union without formal sanction.

text:
Not if he really meant it. Uttered insincerely, such words would be
insult; she would see through his pretence of earnestness, and then
farewell to her for ever. But if his intellectual sympathy became
tinged with passion—and did he discern no possibility of that? An odd
thing were he to fall in love with Rhoda Nunn. Hitherto his ideal had
been a widely different type of woman; he had demanded rare beauty of
face, and the charm of a refined voluptuousness. To be sure, it was but
an ideal; no woman that approached it had ever come within his sphere.
The dream exercised less power over him than a few years ago; perhaps
because his youth was behind him. Rhoda might well represent the desire
of a mature man, strengthened by modern culture and with his senses
fairly subordinate to reason. Heaven forbid that he should ever tie
himself to the tame domestic female; and just as little could he seek
for a mate among the women of society, the creatures all surface, with
empty pates and vitiated blood. No marriage for him, in the common
understanding of the word. He wanted neither offspring nor a “home”.
Rhoda Nunn, if she thought of such things at all, probably desired a
union which would permit her to remain an intellectual being; the
kitchen, the cradle, and the work-basket had no power over her
imagination. As likely as not, however, she was perfectly content with
single life—even regarded it as essential to her purposes. In her face
he read chastity; her eye avoided no scrutiny; her palm was cold.

four o’clock address. The subject had been announced a week ago: “Woman
as an Invader.” An hour earlier than usual work was put aside, and
seats were rapidly arranged for the small audience; it numbered only
thirteen—the girls already on the premises and a few who came
specially. All were aware of the tragedy in which Miss Barfoot had
recently been concerned; her air of sadness, so great a contrast to

As always, she began in the simplest conversational tone. Not long
since she had received an anonymous letter, written by some clerk out
of employment, abusing her roundly for her encouragement of female
competition in the clerkly world. The taste of this epistle was as bad
as its grammar, but they should hear it; she read it all through. Now,
whoever the writer might be, it seemed pretty clear that he was not the
kind of person with whom one could profitably argue; no use in replying
to him, even had he given the opportunity. For all that, his uncivil
attack had a meaning, and there were plenty of people ready to urge his
argument in more respectable terms. “They will tell you that, in
entering the commercial world, you not only unsex yourselves, but do a
grievous wrong to the numberless men struggling hard for bare
sustenance. You reduce salaries, you press into an already overcrowded
field, you injure even your own sex by making it impossible for men to
marry, who, if they earned enough, would be supporting a wife.” To-day,
continued Miss Barfoot, it was not her purpose to debate the economic
aspects of the question. She would consider it from another point of
view, repeating, perhaps, much that she had already said to them on
other occasions, but doing so because these thoughts had just now very
strong possession of her mind.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mary begins her great manifesto on women's invasion of male spheres, opening with a letter from an unemployed clerk attacking her work. This is the novel's most important statement of feminist principle.
enrichment.best_quote: she read it all through... For all that, his uncivil attack had a meaning, and there were plenty of people ready to urge his argument in more respectable terms
enrichment.summary: Mary opens her address by reading an abusive letter from an unemployed clerk criticizing her encouragement of female workplace competition, and uses it as springboard for her argument.

young woman who did his work for smaller payment, doubtless had a
grievance. But, in the miserable disorder of our social state, one

“Follow me carefully. A governess, a nurse, may be the most admirable
of women. I will dissuade no one from following those careers who is
distinctly fitted for them. But these are only a few out of the vast
number of girls who must, if they are not to be despicable persons,
somehow find serious work. Because I myself have had an education in
clerkship, and have most capacity for such employment, I look about for
girls of like mind, and do my best to prepare them for work in offices.
And (here I must become emphatic once more) I am  glad  to have entered
on this course. I am  glad  that I can show girls the way to a career
which my opponents call unwomanly.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mary explains her strategy: she trains women for office work because she believes in their rationality and capacity, and she is 'glad' to enable this 'unwomanly' path.
enrichment.best_quote: I am glad to have entered on this course. I am glad that I can show girls the way to a career which my opponents call unwomanly

“Now see why. Womanly and womanish are two very different words; but
the latter, as the world uses it, has become practically synonymous
with the former. A womanly occupation means, practically, an occupation
that a man disdains. And here is the root of the matter. I repeat that
I am not first of all anxious to keep you supplied with daily bread. I
am a troublesome, aggressive, revolutionary person. I want to do away
with that common confusion of the words womanly and womanish, and I see
very clearly that this can only be effected by an armed movement, an
invasion by women of the spheres which men have always forbidden us to
enter. I am strenuously opposed to that view of us set forth in such
charming language by Mr. Ruskin—for it tells on the side of those men
who think and speak of us in a way the reverse of charming. Were we
living in an ideal world, I think women would not go to sit all day in
offices. But the fact is that we live in a world as far from ideal as
can be conceived. We live in a time of warfare, of revolt. If woman is
no longer to be womanish, but a human being of powers and
responsibilities, she must become militant, defiant. She must push her
claims to the extremity.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mary's masterwork: a sustained polemic against Ruskin, conventional gender norms, and the conflation of 'womanly' with 'womanish.' She calls for militant invasion of male spheres as the only path to female humanity.
enrichment.best_quote: I am a troublesome, aggressive, revolutionary person... women must become militant, defiant. She must push her claims to the extremity
enrichment.summary: Mary launches a sustained attack on Ruskin and conventional femininity, arguing that only militant assertion of women's right to work across all fields can advance civilization.

“An excellent governess, a perfect hospital nurse, do work which is
invaluable; but for our cause of emancipation they are no good—nay,
they are harmful. Men point to them, and say: Imitate these, keep to
your proper world. Our proper world is the world of intelligence, of
honest effort, of moral strength. The old types of womanly perfection
are no longer helpful to us. Like the Church service, which to all but
one person in a thousand has become meaningless gabble by dint of
repetition, these types have lost their effect. They are no longer
educational. We have to ask ourselves: What course of training will
wake women up, make them conscious of their souls, startle them into

“It must be something new, something free from the reproach of
womanliness. I don’t care whether we crowd out the men or not. I don’t
care  what  results, if only women are made strong and self-reliant and
nobly independent! The world must look to its concerns. Most likely we
shall have a revolution in the social order greater than any that yet

text:
“Our abusive correspondent shall do as best he can. He suffers for the
folly of men in all ages. We can’t help it. It is very far from our
wish to cause hardship to any one, but we ourselves are escaping from a
hardship that has become intolerable. We are educating ourselves. There
must be a new type of woman, active in every sphere of life: a new
worker out in the world, a new ruler of the home. Of the old ideal
virtues we can retain many, but we have to add to them those which have
been thought appropriate only in men. Let a woman be gentle, but at the
same time let her be strong; let her be pure of heart, but none the
less wise and instructed. Because we have to set an example to the
sleepy of our sex, we must carry on an active warfare—must be
invaders. Whether woman is the equal of man I neither know nor care. We
are not his equal in size, in weight, in muscle, and, for all I can
say, we may have less power of brain. That has nothing to do with it.
Enough for us to know that our natural growth has been stunted. The
mass of women have always been paltry creatures, and their paltriness
has proved a curse to men. So, if you like to put it in this way, we
are working for the advantage of men as well as for our own. Let the
responsibility for disorder rest on those who have made us despise our
old selves. At any cost—at any cost—we will free ourselves from the
heritage of weakness and contempt!”

If Everard had pleased himself he would have visited the house in
Queen’s Road every other day. As this might not be, he spent a good
deal of his time in other society, not caring to read much, or
otherwise occupy his solitude. Starting with one or two acquaintances
in London, people of means and position, he easily extended his social
sphere. Had he cared to marry, he might, notwithstanding his poverty,
have wooed with fair chance in a certain wealthy family, where two
daughters, the sole children, plain but well-instructed girls, waited
for the men of brains who should appreciate them. So rare in society,
these men of brains, and, alas! so frequently deserted by their wisdom
when it comes to choosing a wife. It being his principle to reflect on
every possibility, Barfoot of course asked himself whether it would not
be reasonable to approach one or other of these young women—the Miss
Brissendens. He needed a larger income; he wanted to travel in a more
satisfactory way than during his late absence. Agnes Brissenden struck
him as a very calm and sensible girl; not at all likely to marry any
one but the man who would be a suitable companion for her, and probably
disposed to look on marriage as a permanent friendship, which must not
be endangered by feminine follies. She had no beauty, but mental powers
above the average—superior, certainly, to her sister’s.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Extended interior monologue revealing Everard's conflicted state: his desire to visit Rhoda constantly, his expansion into London society, his calculation about marrying Agnes Brissenden for money, and his assessment of her as a rational marriage prospect. This passage occurs after Everard has begun visiting Miss Barfoot's house regularly to see Rhoda Nunn, but before he makes his private declaration of love to her. It reveals Everard's internal deliberation about marriage prospects: though he is drawn to Rhoda and visits frequently when he can, he also contemplates a more practical marriage to Agnes Brissenden, a wealthy and intellectually capable woman, as a way to improve his financial circumstances. This moment illustrates the tension between Everard's growing emotional attachment to Rhoda and his rational consideration of conventional matrimonial advantage.

# Context for Chunk

This quotation appears in Paragraph 73 as Everard Barfoot reflects on his growing attraction to Rhoda Nunn during a private conversation with her. The lines, which he recalls from memory, express his desire to provoke her emotionally and physically restrain her—capturing his increasingly intense but conflicted feelings toward her. He recognizes these thoughts as bordering on genuine love, though he initially wished to avoid such serious emotion. The quotation encapsulates his internal struggle between intellectual appreciation of her character and his physical and emotional desire to overcome her resistance.

context:
# Context for Chunk

This passage concludes Rhoda Nunn's private reflections late at night after Everard Barfoot's visit. Having nearly received a declaration of love from him before they were interrupted by other visitors, Rhoda sits alone in the library contemplating his advances. She realizes that despite her intellectual disapproval of his reputation, she is emotionally affected by his attention. The final lines show her decision to neither reject him outright nor encourage him, but rather to wait for him to fully prove the sincerity of his feelings through further declarations of love. This moment represents a turning point where Rhoda acknowledges her long-suppressed desire to experience romantic devotion, viewing his potential pursuit as validation that will ultimately strengthen her resolve to remain unmarried.

Little change had been made in the interior of the house since its
master’s marriage. The dressing-room adjoining the principal
bed-chamber was adapted to Monica’s use, and a few ornaments were added
to the drawing-room. Unlike his deceased brother, Widdowson had the
elements of artistic taste; in furnishing his abode he took counsel
with approved decorators, and at moderate cost had made himself a home
which presented no original features, but gave no offence to a
cultivated eye. The first sight of the rooms pleased Monica greatly.
She declared that all was perfect, nothing need be altered. In those
days, if she had bidden him spend a hundred pounds on reconstruction,
the lover would have obeyed, delighted to hear her express a wish.

Though competence had come to him only after a lifetime of narrow
means, Widdowson felt no temptation to parsimony. Secure in his
all-sufficing income, he grudged no expenditure that could bring

Devon, and Somerset—it lasted about seven weeks—Monica learnt, among

chapter_title:
CHAPTER XV

THE JOYS OF HOME
text:
At the same time he endeavoured to impress her with the gravest sense
of a married woman’s obligations. His raptures, genuine enough, were
sometimes interrupted in the oddest way if Monica chanced to utter a
careless remark of which he could not strictly approve, and such
interruptions frequently became the opportunity for a long and solemn
review of the wifely status. Without much trouble he had brought her
into a daily routine which satisfied him. During the whole of the
morning she was to be absorbed in household cares. In the afternoon he
would take her to walk or drive, and the evening he wished her to spend
either in drawing-room or library, occupied with a book. Monica soon
found that his idea of wedded happiness was that they should always be
together. Most reluctantly he consented to her going any distance
alone, for whatever purpose. Public entertainments he regarded with no
great favour, but when he saw how Monica enjoyed herself at concert or
theatre, he made no objection to indulging her at intervals of a
fortnight or so; his own fondness for music made this compliance
easier. He was jealous of her forming new acquaintances; indifferent to
society himself, he thought his wife should be satisfied with her
present friends, and could not understand why she wished to see them so
often.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Masterwork of characterization and social critique: Gissing lays out Widdowson's entire philosophy of patriarchal control. His absolute insistence on togetherness, distrust of Monica's independence, censure of her professional past, suspicion of her friendships, and religious instrumentalism are all exposed as forms of despotism.
enrichment.best_quote: Never had it occurred to Widdowson that a wife remains an individual, with rights and obligations independent of her wifely condition. Everything he said presupposed his own supremacy; he took for granted that it was his to direct, hers to be guided.
enrichment.summary: Extended exposition detailing Widdowson's controlling marriage philosophy: constant togetherness, control of Monica's movements and friendships, disgust at her professional past, and his unconscious despotism cloaked in gentleness and religious conviction.

context: This passage describes Widdowson's controlling behavior and expectations toward Monica following their marriage. It details his efforts to establish strict domestic routines, his insistence on constant companionship, his reluctance to allow her independence, and his jealous opposition to her maintaining friendships—establishing the fundamental marital conflict that drives the chapter's narrative.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER XV

THE JOYS OF HOME
text:
The girl was docile, and for a time he imagined that there would never
be conflict between his will and hers. Whilst enjoying their holiday
they naturally went everywhere together, and were scarce an hour out of
each other’s presence, day or night. In quiet spots by the seashore,
when they sat in solitude, Widdowson’s tongue was loosened, and he
poured forth his philosophy of life with the happy assurance that
Monica would listen passively. His devotion to her proved itself in a
thousand ways; week after week he grew, if anything, more kind, more
tender; yet in his view of their relations he was unconsciously the
most complete despot, a monument of male autocracy. Never had it
occurred to Widdowson that a wife remains an individual, with rights
and obligations independent of her wifely condition. Everything he said
presupposed his own supremacy; he took for granted that it was his to
direct, hers to be guided. A display of energy, purpose, ambition, on
Monica’s part, which had no reference to domestic pursuits, would have
gravely troubled him; at once he would have set himself to subdue, with
all gentleness, impulses so inimical to his idea of the married state.
It rejoiced him that she spoke with so little sympathy of the
principles supported by Miss Barfoot and Miss Nunn; these persons
seemed to him well-meaning, but grievously mistaken. Miss Nunn he
judged “unwomanly,” and hoped in secret that Monica would not long
remain on terms of friendship with her. Of course his wife’s former
pursuits were an abomination to him; he could not bear to hear them
referred to.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Critical passage revealing the honeymoon phase and Monica's initial docility, while also exposing Widdowson's complete unconsciousness of his own despotism; Gissing's irony is superb.
enrichment.best_quote: yet in his view of their relations he was unconsciously the most complete despot, a monument of male autocracy.
enrichment.summary: During the honeymoon, Monica was docile, and Widdowson grew more tender while remaining utterly oblivious to his absolute dominance; he never conceived that a wife retained independent personhood.

context: This passage appears mid-chapter as paragraph [P42] and provides crucial psychological insight into Widdowson's character and his controlling attitudes toward Monica during their honeymoon. It reveals the fundamental contradiction between his tender devotion and his despotic control, establishes his opposition to Monica's independent friendships with Miss Barfoot and Miss Nunn, and foreshadows the marital conflicts that emerge later in the chapter when Monica begins asserting her desire for freedom and autonomy. The passage explains the ideological foundation of Widdowson's resistance to Monica's requests to visit friends and go out unaccompanied.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER XV

THE JOYS OF HOME
text:
“Woman’s sphere is the home, Monica. Unfortunately girls are often
obliged to go out and earn their living, but this is unnatural, a
necessity which advanced civilization will altogether abolish. You
shall read John Ruskin; every word he says about women is good and
precious. If a woman can neither have a home of her own, nor find
occupation in any one else’s she is deeply to be pitied; her life is
bound to be unhappy. I sincerely believe that an educated woman had
better become a domestic servant than try to imitate the life of a man.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson's monologue quintessentially captures Victorian male ideology: women's natural sphere is the home, work is unnatural, and female independence is pitiful. His invocation of Ruskin and his suggestion that educated women become servants is magnificent satire.
enrichment.best_quote: Woman's sphere is the home, Monica. Unfortunately girls are often obliged to go out and earn their living, but this is unnatural, a necessity which advanced civilization will altogether abolish.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson expounds his ideology that women belong in the home, work is unnatural for them, and he recommends Monica read Ruskin; he suggests educated women should become servants rather than imitate men.

context: This chunk is part of paragraph P43, where Widdowson expresses his rigid Victorian philosophy about women's proper role to his wife Monica. It represents his core belief that women should be confined to domestic life and that work outside the home is unnatural. The passage reflects Widdowson's attempts to control Monica by imposing traditional gender ideology, citing John Ruskin as authority. This speech illustrates the fundamental tension in their marriage: Widdowson's desire to keep Monica as a dutiful homemaker conflicts with her independent nature and past professional life, which he finds abhorrent. The passage encapsulates the patriarchal attitudes that increasingly frustrate Monica and drive the conflict between them.

THE JOYS OF HOME

He believed himself the happiest of men. He had taken a daring step,
but fortune smiled upon him, Monica was all he had imagined in his
love-fever; knowledge of her had as yet brought to light no single
untruth, no trait of character that he could condemn. That she
returned his love he would not and could not doubt. And something she
said to him one day, early in their honeymoon, filled up the measure of
his bliss.

enrichment.summary: Widdowson believes himself the happiest of men, confident in Monica's love and unaware of any character faults in her.

“What a change you have made in my life, Edmund! How much I have to

THE JOYS OF HOME
