text:
Not many people visited this house. Every Wednesday evening, from
half-past eight to eleven, Miss Barfoot was at home to any of her
acquaintances, including her pupils, who chose to call upon her; but
this was in the nature of an association with recognized objects. Of
society in the common sense Miss Barfoot saw very little; she had no
time to sacrifice in the pursuit of idle ceremonies. By the successive
deaths of two relatives, a widowed sister and an uncle, she had come
into possession of a modest fortune; but no thought of a life such as
would have suggested itself to most women in her place ever tempted
her. Her studies had always been of a very positive nature; her
abilities were of a kind uncommon in women, or at all events very
rarely developed in one of her sex. She could have managed a large and
complicated business, could have filled a place on a board of
directors, have taken an active part in municipal government—nay,
perchance in national. And this turn of intellect consisted with many
traits of character so strongly feminine that people who knew her best
thought of her with as much tenderness as admiration. She did not seek
to become known as the leader of a “movement,” yet her quiet work was
probably more effectual than the public career of women who
propagandize for female emancipation. Her aim was to draw from the
overstocked profession of teaching as many capable young women as she
could lay hands on, and to fit them for certain of the pursuits
nowadays thrown open to their sex. She held the conviction that
whatever man could do, woman could do equally well—those tasks only
excepted which demand great physical strength. At her instance, and
with help from her purse, two girls were preparing themselves to be
pharmaceutical chemists; two others had been aided by her to open a
bookseller’s shop; and several who had clerkships in view received an
admirable training at her school in Great Portland Street.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rich, comprehensive exposition of Barfoot's background, values, and educational enterprise: she is an uncommon woman of business acumen and refined character, with progressive ideas about female education and capabilities, yet surprisingly modest impact-seeking.
enrichment.best_quote: She did not seek to become known as the leader of a 'movement,' yet her quiet work was probably more effectual than the public career of women who propagandize for female emancipation.
enrichment.summary: The narrator provides extensive background on Miss Barfoot's financial independence, intellectual abilities, and educational mission: she draws capable young women from teaching to train for new professions through her Great Portland Street school, believing women equal to men except in tasks requiring great strength.

context: This passage appears midway through the chapter and provides crucial background on Miss Barfoot's character, motivations, and work. It comes after the Madden sisters' visit and Mrs. Smallbrook's awkward encounter, and serves as a detailed portrait of Miss Barfoot's philosophy and practical achievements in advancing women's education and employment—establishing her as the chapter's key figure dedicated to female emancipation through practical training rather than public advocacy.

text:
Entering by the private door of a picture-cleaner’s shop, they ascended
to the second story, where two rooms had been furnished like
comfortable offices; two smaller on the floor above served for
dressing-rooms. In one of the offices, typewriting and occasionally
other kinds of work that demanded intelligence were carried on by three
or four young women regularly employed. To superintend this department
was Miss Nunn’s chief duty, together with business correspondence under
the principal’s direction. In the second room Miss Barfoot instructed
her pupils, never more than three being with her at a time. A bookcase
full of works on the Woman Question and allied topics served as a
circulating library; volumes were lent without charge to the members of
this little society. Once a month Miss Barfoot or Miss Nunn, by turns,
gave a brief address on some set subject; the hour was four o’clock,
and about a dozen hearers generally assembled. Both worked very hard.
Miss Barfoot did not look upon her enterprise as a source of pecuniary
profit, but she had made the establishment more than self-supporting.
Her pupils increased in number, and the working department promised
occupation for a larger staff than was at present engaged. The young
women in general answered their friend’s expectations, but of course
there were disappointing instances. One of these had caused Miss
Barfoot special distress. A young girl whom she had released from a
life of much hardship, and who, after a couple of months’ trial, bade
fair to develop noteworthy ability, of a sudden disappeared. She was
without relatives in London, and Miss Barfoot’s endeavours to find her
proved for several weeks very futile. Then came news of her; she was
living as the mistress of a married man. Every effort was made to bring
her back, but the girl resisted; presently she again passed out of
sight, and now more than a year had elapsed since Miss Barfoot’s last
interview with her.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Detailed, vivid account of the school's physical setup and operations; introduction of Bella Royston's tragedy as the climax—a gifted pupil who was seduced by a married man and disappeared into mistressdom, representing both the hope and peril of female independence. Exceptionally significant for the chapter's central conflict.
enrichment.best_quote: A young girl whom she had released from a life of much hardship, and who, after a couple of months' trial, bade fair to develop noteworthy ability, of a sudden disappeared. She was without relatives in London, and Miss Barfoot's endeavours to find her proved for several weeks very futile. Then came news of her; she was living as the mistress of a married man.
enrichment.summary: The narrator describes the school's setup and operations in detail, culminating in the tragic account of Bella Royston: a talented pupil whom Barfoot had removed from hardship, who showed promise, but who abandoned the school to become the mistress of a married man, resisting all efforts to rescue her.

context: This passage describes the physical layout and operations of Miss Barfoot's school at Great Portland Street, where she trains young women in typewriting and clerical work as part of her mission to provide employment opportunities for educated women. It also introduces the case of Bella Royston, a promising pupil who abandoned the school to become the mistress of a married man—a situation that will later provoke a heated debate between Miss Barfoot and her partner Rhoda Nunn about whether to offer the fallen girl redemption or maintain strict moral standards for the school's reputation.

“I don’t, altogether. “The education of women in self-respect.” Very
well. Here is a poor woman whose self-respect has given way under

mistake. The man gives her up, and bids her live as she can; she is

still further. The letter of two lines and an enclosed cheque would as
likely as not plunge her into depths from which she could never be
rescued. It would assure her that there was no hope. On the other hand,
we have it in our power to attempt that very education of which you
speak. She has brains, and doesn’t belong to the vulgar. It seems to me
that you are moved by illogical impulses—and certainly anything but
kind ones.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's masterful counter-argument: she reinterprets Rhoda's logic compassionately—Bella's self-respect is shattered, and the two-line response would guarantee despair and further descent, whereas re-admission offers education and recovery. “Yes, and at a stroke change the whole character of your work. You
never proposed keeping a reformatory. Your aim is to help chosen girls,
who promise to be of some use in the world. This Miss Royston
represents the profitless average—no, she is below the average. Are

But to put her among your chosen pupils is to threaten your whole
undertaking. Let it once become known—and it  would  become
known—that a girl of that character came here, and your usefulness is
at an end. In a year’s time you will have to choose between giving up
the school altogether and making it a refuge for outcasts.”

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“Personal feeling is misleading you,” Rhoda pursued. “Miss Royston had
a certain cleverness, I grant; but do you think I didn’t know that she
would never become what you hoped? All her spare time was given to
novel-reading. If every novelist could be strangled and thrown into the
sea we should have some chance of reforming women. The girl’s nature
was corrupted with sentimentality, like that of all but every woman who
is intelligent enough to read what is called the best fiction, but not
intelligent enough to understand its vice. Love—love—love; a
sickening sameness of vulgarity. What is more vulgar than the ideal of
novelists? They won’t represent the actual world; it would be too dull
for their readers. In real life, how many men and women  fall in love ?
Not one in every ten thousand, I am convinced. Not one married pair in
ten thousand have felt for each other as two or three couples do in
every novel. There is the sexual instinct, of course, but that is quite
a different thing; the novelists daren’t talk about that. The paltry
creatures daren’t tell the one truth that would be profitable. The
result is that women imagine themselves noble and glorious when they
are most near the animals. This Miss Royston—when she rushed off to
perdition, ten to one she had in mind some idiot heroine of a book. Oh,
I tell you that you are losing sight of your first duty. There are
people enough to act the good Samaritan;  you  have quite another task
in life. It is your work to train and encourage girls in a path as far
as possible from that of the husband-hunter. Let them marry later, if
they must; but at all events you will have cleared their views on the
subject of marriage, and put them in a position to judge the man who
offers himself. You will have taught them that marriage is an alliance
of intellects—not a means of support, or something more ignoble still.
But to do this with effect you must show yourself relentless to female
imbecility. If a girl gets to know that you have received back such a
person as Miss Royston she will be corrupted by your spirit of
charity—corrupted, at all events, for our purposes. The endeavour to
give women a new soul is so difficult that we can’t be cumbered by
side-tasks, such as fishing foolish people out of the mud they have
walked into. Charity for human weakness is all very well in its place,
but it is precisely one of the virtues that you must  not  teach. You
have to set an example of the sterner qualities—to discourage anything
that resembles sentimentalism. And think if you illustrate in your own
behaviour a sympathy for the very vice of character we are trying our
hardest to extirpate!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's passionate harangue: she attacks Bella's sentimentality, blames novels for corrupting women, defends a strict ideal, frames the work as transformation of female nature itself; reveals her ideological intensity, anti-romantic fervor, and contempt for 'female imbecility'—the chapter's most extended and vivid expression of Rhoda's radical asceticism.
enrichment.best_quote: If every novelist could be strangled and thrown into the sea we should have some chance of reforming women.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda argues that Bella was corrupted by sentimental novels that misrepresent love; she attacks sentimentality and the romantic ideal as enemies of female progress; warns that readmitting Bella would teach charity instead of the stern virtues needed for true emancipation.

context: **Context:** After Miss Barfoot receives a letter from Bella Royston, a former pupil who abandoned her studies to become a married man's mistress, she considers helping the girl return to work at the school. Rhoda Nunn vehemently opposes this decision, delivering this passionate argument against Miss Barfoot's charitable impulse. Rhoda contends that novelistic sentimentality corrupted Miss Royston's judgment, that readmitting her would compromise the school's mission to educate women in self-respect and rational thinking about marriage, and that Miss Barfoot must prioritize her duty to train girls to value intellectual alliance over romantic love.

chapter_title:

“We differ a good deal, Rhoda, on certain points which as a rule would
never come up to interfere with our working in harmony. You have come
to dislike the very thought of marriage—and everything of that kind. I
think it’s a danger you ought to have avoided. True, we wish to prevent
girls from marrying just for the sake of being supported, and from
degrading themselves as poor Bella Royston has done; but surely between
ourselves we can admit that the vast majority of women would lead a
wasted life if they did not marry.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's measured rebuttal: she and Rhoda differ fundamentally on marriage's necessity; Barfoot defends human nature against institutional critique; suggests Rhoda's rejection of marriage is both intellectually extreme and personally dangerous.

“Don’t you blame the institution of marriage with what is chargeable to

“There again we differ. You are quite mistaken in your ideas of how the
mind is influenced. The misery of Bella Royston would not in the least
affect any other girl’s way of thinking about the destiny of her sex.
We must avoid exaggeration. If our friends get to think of us as
fanatics, all our usefulness is over. The ideal we set up must be
human. Do you think now that we know one single girl who in her heart
believes it is better never to love and never to marry?”

chapter_title:

“No, my dear. We happen to be going to the root of things, that’s all.
Perhaps it’s as well to do so now and then. Oh, I admire you immensely,
Rhoda. You are the ideal adversary of those care-nothing and
believe-nothing women who keep the world back. But don’t prepare for
yourself a woeful disillusion.”

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“Winifred has much good sense,” admitted the other. “I think she is in
as little danger as any girl we know. But it wouldn’t startle me if she
made the most lamentable mistake. Certainly I don’t fear it. The girls
of our class are not like the uneducated, who, for one reason or
another, will marry almost any man rather than remain single. They have
at all events personal delicacy. But what I insist upon is, that
Winifred would rather marry than not. And we must carefully bear that
fact in mind. A strained ideal is as bad, practically, as no ideal at
all. Only the most exceptional girl will believe it her duty to remain
single as an example and support to what we call the odd women; yet
 that  is the most human way of urging what you desire. By taking up
the proud position that a woman must be altogether independent of
sexual things, you damage your cause. Let us be glad if we put a few of
them in the way of living single with no more discontent than an
unmarried man experiences.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's long, nuanced final statement: she defends Winifred's good sense while insisting she would *prefer* marriage, acknowledges the danger of strained ideals, and defines the best approach as one that prepares girls to judge marriage rationally while accepting its probability—humanistic feminism versus ascetic purism.
enrichment.best_quote: By taking up the proud position that a woman must be altogether independent of sexual things, you damage your cause. Let us be glad if we put a few of them in the way of living single with no more discontent than an unmarried man experiences.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot defends Winifred's capacity for judgment while asserting that most women would prefer marriage; she argues that a strained ascetic ideal damages feminism and that the true goal is contentment for the unmarried, not enforced celibacy.

context: This passage occurs late in the chapter during a private conversation between Miss Barfoot and Rhoda Nunn after the day's pupils and staff have departed. Miss Barfoot is responding to Rhoda's argument against taking back Bella Royston, a fallen girl. The conversation has escalated into a broader debate about the proper ideals to promote to their female students—specifically whether to advocate for women's independence from marriage and sexuality, or to acknowledge that most women will naturally desire to marry. Miss Barfoot urges moderation and pragmatism, cautioning Rhoda against promoting an overly "strained ideal" that is unrealistic and counterproductive to their cause of female emancipation.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“Surely that’s an unfortunate comparison,” said Rhoda coldly. “What man
lives in celibacy? Consider that unmentionable fact, and then say
whether I am wrong in refusing to forgive Miss Royston. Women’s battle
is not only against themselves. The necessity of the case demands what
you call a strained ideal. I am seriously convinced that before the
female sex can be raised from its low level there will have to be a
widespread revolt against sexual instinct. Christianity couldn’t spread
over the world without help of the ascetic ideal, and this great
movement for woman’s emancipation must also have its ascetics.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's final major statement: she challenges Barfoot's comparison, pointing out that men's celibacy is rare due to sexual freedom; she frames women's emancipation as requiring ascetic resistance to sexual instinct, analogous to Christianity's ascetic ideal. The ideological climax of the debate.
enrichment.best_quote: The necessity of the case demands what you call a strained ideal. I am seriously convinced that before the female sex can be raised from its low level there will have to be a widespread revolt against sexual instinct.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda rejects Barfoot's comparison, pointing out that men escape celibacy through sexual access; she insists that female emancipation requires ascetic resistance to sexual instinct, framing it as necessary as Christianity's ascetic ideal.

context: This passage occurs during a heated debate between Miss Barfoot and Rhoda Nunn about whether to rehire Bella Royston, a former pupil who became the mistress of a married man. Rhoda argues passionately that forgiving such moral lapses would undermine their mission to educate women in self-restraint and independence from marriage. Here, she defends her uncompromising stance by asserting that women's emancipation requires an ascetic ideal comparable to Christianity's, demanding that women renounce sexual instinct entirely—a standard she notes men are never held to.

chapter_title:

“I can’t declare that you are wrong in that. Who knows? But it isn’t
good policy to preach it to our young disciples.”

enrichment.summary: Barfoot grants that Rhoda may be right philosophically but insists such ascetic ideals should not be taught to their pupils.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“My dear,” said the elder woman gravely, “believe me that the less we
talk or think about such things the better for the peace of us all. The
odious fault of working-class girls, in town and country alike, is that
they are absorbed in preoccupation with their animal nature. We, thanks
to our education and the tone of our society, manage to keep that in
the background. Don’t interfere with this satisfactory state of things.
Be content to show our girls that it is their duty to lead a life of
effort—to earn their bread and to cultivate their minds. Simply ignore
marriage—that’s the wisest. Behave as if the thing didn’t exist. You
will do positive harm by taking the other course—the aggressive
course.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's long, final statement: she urges silence on sexual matters, observes that educated women are fortunately distanced from 'animal nature' through culture and education, and warns against Rhoda's aggressive course. Reveals tension between female emancipation and domestication.
enrichment.best_quote: Simply ignore marriage—that's the wisest. Behave as if the thing didn't exist.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot advises silence on marriage and sexual matters, noting that educated women are fortuitously protected from base preoccupation with the animal; she warns against Rhoda's aggressive strategy.

context: Miss Barfoot advises Rhoda Nunn to avoid aggressive preaching about sexual restraint and marriage to their female pupils. She argues that educated women should simply ignore the topic of marriage altogether and focus instead on teaching girls to be self-sufficient and intellectually cultivated, warning that Rhoda's strident idealism about rejecting sexual instinct will do more harm than good to their educational mission.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE

the spot with horse and trap. These were not, as he presently informed
Monica, his own property, but hired from a livery stable, according to
his custom.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica keeps her appointment despite doubtful weather; notes that Widdowson has hired the trap and horse.
enrichment.summary: Monica meets Widdowson at the appointed location; he is waiting with a hired horse and trap.

context: Monica agrees to meet Widdowson at Regent's Park on Sunday for a drive. Despite uncertain weather, she arrives at the appointed time and meets him with a hired horse and trap, beginning their excursion into Surrey.

text:
“It won’t rain,” he exclaimed, gazing at the sky. “It  shan’t  rain!
These few hours are too precious to me.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson's optimistic assertion about the weather; shows his eagerness and desire to will favorable conditions.
enrichment.best_quote: It shan't rain!
enrichment.summary: Widdowson asserts confidently that it will not rain, emphasizing how precious these hours with Monica are to him.

context: Monica has agreed to go on a drive with Widdowson on Sunday afternoon. As they prepare to depart in a hired horse and trap, Widdowson anxiously assures Monica that the threatening sky will not bring rain, as these hours with her are too precious to him.

text:
“It would be very awkward if it  did ,” Monica replied, in merry
humour, as they drove along.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica's merry response suggesting rain would be awkward; light banter showing her in better spirits.
enrichment.summary: Monica replies in merry humor that it would indeed be awkward if it rained.

context: Monica has agreed to go on a drive with Widdowson in a hired horse and trap. As they set out from Regent's Park on a doubtful day, Widdowson insists confidently that it won't rain, declaring these hours too precious to him. Monica responds with light humor about the possibility of rain interrupting their outing.

text:
The sky threatened till sundown, but Widdowson was able to keep
declaring that rain would not come. He took a south-westward course,
crossed Waterloo Bridge, and thence by the highways made for Herne
Hill. Monica observed that he made a short detour to avoid Walworth
Road. She asked his reason.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica observes Widdowson taking a southwestward route toward Herne Hill and asks why he avoids Walworth Road; prompts his emotional response about the location.
enrichment.summary: Monica notices that Widdowson deliberately takes a detour to avoid Walworth Road and asks him why.

context: Monica accepts Widdowson's invitation for a drive in Surrey in his hired horse and trap. As they travel southwestward toward Herne Hill to see his house, Monica notices he deliberately avoids Walworth Road, the location of her former shop where she endured difficult employment.

text: “I hate the road!” Widdowson answered, with vehemence.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson's emphatic response; shows his intense feeling about the street.
enrichment.best_quote: I hate the road!
enrichment.summary: Widdowson responds with vehemence that he hates the road.

context: Monica accepts Widdowson's invitation for a carriage drive through Surrey. As they travel toward Herne Hill, Widdowson deliberately avoids Walworth Road—the street where Monica previously worked as a shop assistant—expressing his hatred of the road because of her suffering there and his anguish while she was employed in that degrading position.

text: “You hate it?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica's simple question; routine clarification.
enrichment.summary: Monica asks why he hates it.

context: Monica and Widdowson are driving through Surrey. When he deliberately avoids Walworth Road, Monica asks why, and he responds with vehement emotion that he hates the road because she suffered working there as a shop-girl.

text:
“Because you slaved and suffered there. If I had the power, I would
destroy it—every house. Many a time,” he added, in a lower voice,
“when you were lying asleep, I walked up and down there in horrible
misery.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson's passionate condemnation of Walworth Road and revelation that he walked there in misery while Monica slept shows obsessive surveillance and protectiveness; reveals emotional intensity.
enrichment.best_quote: Many a time when you were lying asleep, I walked up and down there in horrible misery.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson explains that he hates the road because Monica suffered there; he reveals that he walked the street many times in misery while she slept.

context: Widdowson expresses his hatred of Walworth Road, where Monica worked as a shop-girl, revealing that he had walked the street in misery while she slept, deeply disturbed by her suffering and the unsuitable environment of her employment.

text: “Just because I had to stand at a counter?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica's challenging question; routine dialogue clarifying Widdowson's objection.
enrichment.summary: Monica asks if it is merely because she stood at a counter.

context: Monica and Widdowson are driving together in Surrey. Widdowson expresses his hatred of Walworth Road, the street where Monica worked as a shop-girl, revealing he walked there in misery while she slept. Monica responds defensively to his criticism of her former employment.

text:
“Not only that. It wasn’t fit for you to work in that way—but the
people about you! I hated every face of man or woman that passed along
the street.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson elaborates on his hatred of the street and the people in it; reveals his class consciousness and possessiveness.
enrichment.best_quote: I hated every face of man or woman that passed along the street.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson clarifies that it is not only the work itself but the people, whose faces he hated, knowing Monica was exposed to them.

context: Widdowson expresses his disgust at Monica's former employment in the shop on Walworth Road, revealing his possessive feelings and emotional distress over her working conditions and the people she encountered there.

text: “I didn’t like the society.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica's simple agreement; routine dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Monica agrees that she did not enjoy the society of the shop.

context: Monica and Widdowson are driving through Surrey. He expresses his hatred of Walworth Road, where Monica worked as a shop-girl, saying he walked there in misery knowing she suffered there. Monica responds that she didn't like the society of that place, acknowledging his concern about her working conditions.

text:
“I should hope not. Of course, I know you didn’t. Why did you ever come
to such a place?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson pressures Monica with a critical question about her reasons for coming to London; shows his disapproval.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson asks why Monica ever came to such a place, implying his disapproval of her choice.

context: Monica and Widdowson are on a drive through Surrey. When Monica mentions she left shop work because she was tired of dull country life, Widdowson questions why she would have come to work in such an undesirable place, showing disapproval of her past employment in the shop.

text: There was severity rather than sympathy in his look.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Narrator notes Widdowson's severe rather than sympathetic expression; characterizes his judgment.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson's expression shows severity rather than sympathy.

context: Monica and Widdowson are driving through Surrey. He expresses hatred for Walworth Road where Monica worked as a shop-girl, asking if she needed excitement in her life. When she admits she left the country because it was dull, his expression becomes severe rather than sympathetic.

text:
“I was tired of the dull country life,” Monica replied frankly. “And
then I didn’t know what the shops and the people were like.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica honestly explains her reasons for leaving Somerset and coming to London; reveals her motivations and naiveté.
enrichment.best_quote: I was tired of the dull country life.
enrichment.summary: Monica frankly admits she was tired of dull country life and did not know what the shops and city people would be like.

context: Monica explains to Widdowson during their carriage drive why she left Somerset for London to work in the shop at Walworth Road, admitting she sought change from rural monotony despite not understanding what urban shop life would entail.

text: “Do you need a life of excitement?” he asked, with a sidelong glance.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson probes Monica's need for excitement; shows his controlling interest in her motivations.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson asks if Monica needs a life of excitement, his tone and glance implying disapproval.

context: Monica and Widdowson are on a drive through Surrey. He expresses his hatred of Walworth Road, where Monica worked in the shop, and questions her about why she left country life for the excitement of London, asking if she needs excitement in her life.

text: “Excitement? No, but one must have change.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica clarifies she wants change, not excitement; shows her practical orientation.
enrichment.summary: Monica denies needing excitement but maintains that one must have change.

context: Monica and Widdowson are on a carriage drive through Surrey. When Widdowson criticizes her past work at the shop and asks if she needs a life of excitement, Monica responds that she doesn't seek excitement but rather needs change, explaining why she left her country home for London.

text:
When they reached Herne Hill, Widdowson became silent, and presently he
allowed the horse to walk.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Transition paragraph noting Widdowson becomes silent and slows the horse; marks a shift in mood.
enrichment.summary: When they reach Herne Hill, Widdowson becomes silent and allows the horse to walk.

context: Monica and Widdowson are on a drive together in Surrey. Widdowson has been talking tenderly to Monica throughout their journey, and they are approaching his house at Herne Hill, which he wants to show her.

text: “That is my house, Miss Madden—the right-hand one.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson points out his house; a significant moment revealing his domestic aspirations and desire to include Monica in his life.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson points out his house to Monica.

context: Monica is on a drive with Widdowson through Surrey. He points out his house at Herne Hill, a modest villa he has owned and cherished, as part of his effort to win her affection and demonstrate his respectability as a potential husband.

text:
Monica looked, and saw two little villas, built together with stone
facings, porches at the doors and ornamented gables.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Describes Widdowson's modest house with stone facings and ornamented gables; establishes the setting.
enrichment.summary: Monica observes two modest villas built together with stone facings and ornamented gables.

context: Monica and Widdowson are on a drive through Surrey. Widdowson points out his own house at Herne Hill, a modest two-villa structure, as they pass by in the carriage.

text:
“I only wanted to show it you,” he added quickly. “There’s nothing
pretty or noticeable about it, and it isn’t at all grandly furnished.
My old housekeeper and one servant manage to keep it in order.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson disclaims any grandeur in the house but reveals his household staff and domestic arrangements; shows his class position.
enrichment.best_quote: My old housekeeper and one servant manage to keep it in order.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson remarks that the house is not grand and is simply furnished, maintained by an old housekeeper and one servant.

context: Widdowson shows Monica his house at Herne Hill during their carriage drive in Surrey, downplaying its elegance while revealing his pride in owning property and his hopes that she might one day share it as his wife.

text: They passed, and Monica did not allow herself to look back.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica's refusal to look back at the house; brief action note.
enrichment.summary: Monica deliberately does not look back at the house as they pass.

context: Monica and Widdowson are driving past his house at Herne Hill. He has just pointed it out to her, explaining his pride in owning it and his hopes of sharing it with someone. After he shows her the property, they continue on without stopping, and Monica deliberately avoids looking back at it.

text: “I think it’s a nice house,” she said presently.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica offers a polite compliment; routine dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Monica says she thinks it is a nice house.

context: Monica and Widdowson are on a carriage drive through Surrey. Widdowson shows her his house at Herne Hill, a modest villa he has owned for some years. Monica responds with this comment about the house after he points it out to her.

text:
“All my life I have wished to have a house of my own, but I didn’t dare
to hope I ever should. Men in general don’t seem to care so long as
they have lodgings that suit them—I mean unmarried men. But I always
wanted to live alone—without strangers, that is to say. I told you
that I am not very sociable. When I got my house, I was like a child
with a toy; I couldn’t sleep for satisfaction. I used to walk all over
it, day after day, before it was furnished. There was something that
delighted me in the sound of my footsteps on the staircases and the
bare floors. Here I shall live and die, I kept saying to myself. Not in
solitude, I hoped. Perhaps I might meet some one—”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson's long, poignant monologue about his lifelong wish for a home of his own, his delight in its possession, and his hope for companionship reveals his deep emotional needs and romantic intentions; superb character insight.
enrichment.best_quote: All my life I have wished to have a house of my own, but I didn't dare to hope I ever should. Here I shall live and die, I kept saying to myself. Not in solitude, I hoped. Perhaps I might meet some one—
enrichment.summary: Widdowson confesses that owning a house has been a lifelong dream; he describes his joy in its acquisition and his walks through empty rooms, expressing his hope that someone might share it with him.

context: Widdowson takes Monica on a drive through Surrey. As they reach Herne Hill, he shows her his house and reveals his long-held desire to own his own home. He explains how he cherished the solitude of his new house but always hoped to share it with someone, hinting at his desire for marriage and companionship.

text:
Monica interrupted him to ask a question about some object in the
landscape. He answered her very briefly, and for a long time neither
spoke. Then the girl, glancing at him with a smile of apology, said in
a gentle tone—

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica interrupts Widdowson's confession; shows her discomfort with his emotional disclosure.
enrichment.summary: Monica interrupts Widdowson's monologue to ask about a landscape feature.

context: Monica and Widdowson are on a drive through the Surrey countryside. Widdowson has been showing her his house at Herne Hill and beginning to express his romantic feelings and hopes for their future together. Monica interrupts his sentimental reflections about the house to redirect the conversation, creating a moment of tension before she gently encourages him to continue speaking about his home.

text:
“You were telling me how the house pleased you. Have you still the same
pleasure in living there?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica gently redirects Widdowson back to his narrative with an apologetic smile; shows her desire to hear his story despite her earlier interruption.
enrichment.summary: Monica offers a gentle apology and asks Widdowson to continue about the pleasure he found in his house.

context: Monica and Widdowson are on a drive through Surrey. He has just shown her his house at Herne Hill and begun to confess his hopes of not living there alone. Monica interrupts him with a question about the landscape, then politely returns to his previous topic with this gentle inquiry, allowing him to continue expressing his feelings toward her.

text:
“Yes. But lately I have been hoping—I daren’t say more. You will
interrupt me again.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson's response indicates he was about to propose or approach a marriage proposal but was interrupted; hints at his near-confession.
enrichment.best_quote: I daren't say more. You will interrupt me again.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson indicates he has something more to say but fears being interrupted again.

context: Monica and Widdowson are on a drive through Surrey. He has shown her his house at Herne Hill and is attempting to express his romantic feelings toward her, but keeps hesitating or being interrupted. Here he is trying to continue confessing his hopes regarding their potential marriage, but fears Monica will deflect the conversation again as she has done before.

text: “Which way are we going now, Mr. Widdowson?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica's deflection; routine dialogue changing subject.
enrichment.summary: Monica asks Widdowson which way they are now going.

context: Monica and Widdowson are on a drive through Surrey in his hired trap. He has just shown her his house at Herne Hill and made an emotional plea about his loneliness and hopes of marriage. As the evening progresses and the weather improves, Monica redirects his intense personal conversation by asking about their route, attempting to steer away from his marriage proposal.

text:
“To Streatham, then on to Carshalton. At five o’clock we will use our
right as travellers, and get some innkeeper to make tea for us. Look,
the sun is trying to break through; we shall have a fine evening yet.
May I, without rudeness, say that you look better since you left that
abominable place.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson describes their route to Streatham and Carshalton and proposes tea; he compliments Monica's improved appearance, revealing his continued focus on her transformation.
enrichment.best_quote: You look better since you left that abominable place.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson outlines their route and proposes stopping for tea at five o'clock; he remarks that Monica looks better since leaving Walworth Road.

context: Widdowson is driving Monica through Surrey in his hired trap, showing her the countryside and his house at Herne Hill. As they continue their journey southward toward Streatham and Carshalton, he makes pleasant observations about the weather and her improved appearance since leaving her shop work, while planning a tea stop along the way.

text: “Oh, I feel better.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica's simple agreement; routine response.
enrichment.summary: Monica confirms that she feels better.

context: Monica reassures Widdowson that she feels better since leaving her shop job at Walworth Road during their carriage drive through Surrey.

text:
After keeping his look fixed for a long time on the horse’s ears,
Widdowson turned gravely to his companion.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Transition noting Widdowson's grave demeanor as he turns to a new subject; marks a shift to more important conversation.
enrichment.summary: After a long look at the horse's ears, Widdowson turns gravely to address Monica.

context: During a carriage drive through Surrey, Widdowson prepares to ask Monica about meeting his sister-in-law, marking a shift in their conversation from casual observation of the landscape to a more serious personal matter as he gathers courage to press his courtship further.

text:
“I told you about my sister-in-law. Would you be willing to make her
acquaintance?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson raises the delicate matter of meeting his sister-in-law; tests Monica's willingness to integrate into his social world.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson asks if Monica would be willing to meet his sister-in-law.

context: Widdowson asks Monica if she will meet his sister-in-law during their drive through Surrey, as part of his attempt to make their relationship more formal and introduce her to people he knows. Monica refuses this request, unwilling to take steps that would publicly commit her to an engagement before she is ready.

text:
“I don’t feel able to do that, Mr. Widdowson,” Monica answered with
decision.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica's firm refusal reveals her caution about deeper commitment; shows her unwillingness to be drawn further into Widdowson's life.
enrichment.best_quote: I don't feel able to do that, Mr. Widdowson.
enrichment.summary: Monica decidedly refuses, stating she does not feel able to make such an acquaintance.

context: Monica refuses Widdowson's request to meet his sister-in-law, asserting her independence and unwillingness to formalize their relationship prematurely during their carriage drive through Surrey.

text:
Prepared for this reply, he began a long and urgent persuasion. It was
useless; Monica listened quietly, but without sign of yielding. The
subject dropped, and they talked of indifferent things.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson attempts prolonged persuasion but ultimately accepts Monica's refusal; shows his respect for her wishes despite his desires.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson makes a long and urgent persuasive attempt, but Monica listens quietly without yielding; they move on to other topics.

context: Widdowson asks Monica if she would be willing to meet his sister-in-law. Monica refuses firmly. He attempts to persuade her at length, but she remains unmoved, and they move on to other topics of conversation.

text:
On the homeward drive, when the dull sky grew dusk about them, and the
suburban street-lamps began to show themselves in long glimmering
lines, Widdowson returned with shamefaced courage to the subject which
for some hours had been in abeyance.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Transition noting the homeward journey and Widdowson's return to the marriage proposal subject; marks escalation of his intentions.
enrichment.summary: On the homeward drive at dusk, as street-lamps begin to light, Widdowson returns to the subject that has been in abeyance.

context: Monica and Widdowson are returning from their first outing together—a drive through Surrey. As evening falls, Widdowson finally broaches the question he has been avoiding all day: he asks Monica directly to marry him, initiating a crucial conversation about their unconventional relationship and her conditions for accepting his proposal.

text:
“I can’t part from you this evening without a word of hope to remember.
You know that I want you to be my wife. Will you tell me if there is
anything I can say or do to make your consent possible? Have you any
doubt of me?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson makes his direct proposal of marriage, asking Monica to identify any obstacle to her acceptance; a crucial turning point in the novel.
enrichment.best_quote: I can't part from you this evening without a word of hope to remember. You know that I want you to be my wife.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson directly proposes marriage to Monica and asks what he can say or do to make her consent possible.

context: On their first outing together, Widdowson expresses his desire to marry Monica and asks her to consider his proposal, seeking reassurance about her doubts regarding his character and sincerity.

text: “No doubt whatever of your sincerity.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica assures Widdowson she has no doubt of his sincerity; standard response showing trust.
enrichment.summary: Monica confirms she has no doubt of his sincerity.

context: Monica reassures Widdowson that she has no doubts about his sincerity regarding his marriage proposal, during their carriage ride through Surrey when he asks if she distrusts him.

text:
“In one sense, I am still a stranger to you. Will you give me the
opportunity of making things between us more regular? Will you allow me

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson proposes becoming acquainted in an ordinary way and meeting her friends to make their relationship more regular; suggests legitimate courtship.
enrichment.best_quote: Will you allow me to meet some friend of yours whom you trust?
enrichment.summary: Widdowson asks if they might become acquainted in an ordinary way and if he might meet a trusted friend of hers to make their relationship more proper.

context: Widdowson proposes marriage to Monica during their drive in Surrey, asking to meet one of her friends to make their relationship more formal and socially acceptable before she commits to becoming his wife.

text: “I had rather you didn’t yet.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica refuses to involve friends; shows her desire to keep her relationship with Widdowson private.
enrichment.summary: Monica declines, preferring not to involve friends yet.

context: Monica refuses Widdowson's request to meet one of her friends to make their relationship more formal, as she fears it would obligate her to announce an engagement she is not ready to commit to.

text: “You wish to know still more of me, personally?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson asks if Monica wants to know him better personally; routine clarifying question.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson asks if she wishes to know him still more personally.

context: Monica is on a drive with Widdowson, who has just asked her to marry him. She has refused to introduce him to her friends or make their relationship official, saying she needs to know him better first. This line is his clarification of her position as they discuss the terms of their continued acquaintance.

text:
“Yes—I think I must know you much better before I can consent to any
step of that kind.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica confirms she must know him much better before consenting; shows her caution about marriage.
enrichment.summary: Monica affirms that she must know him much better before consenting to any engagement.

context: Monica refuses Widdowson's proposal of marriage during their evening drive in Surrey, insisting she needs to know him better before making any commitment, while he pressures her to formalize their relationship by introducing her to his family.

text:
“But,” he urged, “if we became acquaintances in the ordinary way, and
knew each other’s friends, wouldn’t that be most satisfactory to you?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson argues for ordinary acquaintance through friends as a satisfactory approach; reveals his logic for legitimacy.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson contends that becoming acquainted ordinarily and knowing each other's friends would be most satisfactory.

context: Widdowson proposes that Monica introduce him to her friends and allow their relationship to become public and formal, arguing this would be the most satisfactory arrangement. Monica resists, explaining that revealing their secret courtship would obligate her to announce an engagement she is not yet ready to make.

text:
“It might be. But you forget that so much would have to be explained. I

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica articulates the social complications: revealing their unusual relationship would force her into an engagement or be seen as improper; reveals the novel's class anxieties about female conduct.
enrichment.best_quote: I have behaved very strangely. If I told everything to my friends I should leave myself no choice.
enrichment.summary: Monica explains that much would have to be explained; to tell friends everything would leave her no choice but to declare herself engaged.

context: Monica refuses Widdowson's suggestion that they become acquainted through her friends, explaining that revealing their unconventional private meetings would force her into an engagement before she is ready to commit.

text:
“Oh, why not? You would be absolutely free. I could no more than try to
recommend myself to you. If I am so unhappy as to fail, how would you
be anything but quite free?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Widdowson attempts to reassure Monica that she would remain free; routine dialogue offering reassurance.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson argues that she would be free and that he could only try to recommend himself.

context: Widdowson is trying to convince Monica to introduce him to her friends and make their relationship official. He argues that even if he fails to win her approval through such introductions, she would remain completely free to refuse him. This occurs during their drive in Surrey as he presses her to allow him to meet someone she trusts, despite her reluctance to formalize their unconventional courtship.

text:
“But surely you must understand me. In this position, I must either not
speak of you at all, or make it known that I am engaged to you. I can’t

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica's forceful articulation of her position reveals the paradox facing women: in an engagement, she would not be free; without revelation, she appears immodest. Central to the novel's gender critique.
enrichment.best_quote: In this position, I must either not speak of you at all, or make it known that I am engaged to you. I can't have it taken for granted that I am engaged to you when I don't wish to be.

context: Monica refuses Widdowson's request to introduce her to his family or make their relationship official, explaining that she cannot appear engaged without intending to be, and fears her sisters would judge her as immodest for conducting an unofficial courtship.

text: Widdowson’s head drooped; he set his lips in a hard gloomy expression.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Narrator notes Widdowson's drooping head and gloomy expression; shows his emotional response to Monica's refusal.
enrichment.summary: Widdowson's demeanor becomes despondent; he sets his lips in a hard, gloomy expression.

context: Monica refuses Widdowson's proposal to introduce her to his sister-in-law and make their relationship more formal. When he presses her to allow him to meet one of her friends to make things "more regular," she explains her difficult position: she cannot introduce him to her sisters without either concealing him entirely or appearing engaged. She argues that their unconventional meeting has forced her into this predicament, and she needs time to know him better before committing to marriage. As she speaks earnestly about the unfairness of social conventions and her genuine uncertainty about her feelings, Widdowson reacts with disappointment and gloom at her continued resistance to formalizing their courtship.

text:
“I have behaved very imprudently,” continued the girl. But I don’t
see—I can’t see—what else I could have done. Things are so badly
arranged. It wasn’t possible for us to be introduced by any one who
knew us both, so I had either to break off your acquaintance after that
first conversation, or conduct myself as I have been doing. I think
it’s a very hard position. My sisters would call me an immodest girl,
but I don’t think it is true. I may perhaps come to feel you as a girl
ought to when she marries, and how else can I tell unless I meet you
and talk with you? And your position is just the same. I don’t blame
you for a moment; I think it would be ridiculous to blame you. Yet we
have gone against the ordinary rule, and people would make us suffer
for it—or me, at all events.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Monica's lengthy explanation of their situation reveals her self-awareness, her justification for unconventional behavior, and her hope that love might grow; a superb character moment and statement of feminist principle.
enrichment.best_quote: I may perhaps come to feel you as a girl ought to when she marries, and how else can I tell unless I meet you and talk with you? And your position is just the same. I don't blame you for a moment; I think it would be ridiculous to blame you. Yet we have gone against the ordinary rule, and people would make us suffer for it—or me, at all events.
enrichment.summary: Monica defends their unconventional conduct as necessary and expresses her hope that love might develop through acquaintance; she acknowledges the social penalty women face for such behavior.

context: Monica defends her unconventional courtship with Widdowson during their carriage ride, explaining that their unorthodox meeting and continued secret correspondence were necessary given their unusual circumstances, and justifying her behavior as neither immodest nor blameworthy while acknowledging the social disapproval they would face if their relationship became known.

text:
Her voice at the close was uncertain. Widdowson looked at her with eyes

Dressed, like the hostess, in black, and without ornaments of any kind
save a silver buckle at her waist, Rhoda seemed to have endeavoured to
liken herself to the suggestion of her name by the excessive plainness
with which she had arranged her hair; its tight smoothness was nothing

“My friend Poppleton was one of the most delightful men—perhaps the
best and kindest I ever knew, and so overflowing with natural wit and
humour that there was no resisting his cheerful influence. To the
amazement of every one who knew him, he married perhaps the dullest
woman he could have found. Mrs. Poppleton not only never made a joke,
but couldn’t understand what joking meant. Only the flattest literalism
was intelligible to her; she could follow nothing but the very macadam
of conversation—had no palate for anything but the suet-pudding of
talk.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's extended, darkly comic monologue on Poppleton's marriage reveals his wit, contempt for intellectual incompatibility, and implicit critique of marriage as torment. The passage is both entertaining and thematically rich, suggesting that women's ignorance drives men mad.

Mrs. Poppleton not only never made a joke, but couldn't understand what joking meant. Only the flattest literalism was intelligible to her; she could follow nothing but the very macadam of conversation—had no palate for anything but the suet-pudding of talk.
enrichment.summary: Everard paints a vivid, contemptuous portrait of Mrs. Poppleton's intellectual incapacity, characterizing her as unable to understand wit, jokes, or anything beyond literal conversation.

text:
“Yes,” he continued, “she was by birth a lady—which made the
infliction harder to bear. Poor old Poppleton! Again and again I have
heard him—what do you think?—laboriously  explaining  jests to her.
That was a trial, as you may imagine. There we sat, we three, in the
unbeautiful little parlour—for they were anything but rich. Poppleton
would say something that convulsed me with laughter—in spite of my
efforts, for I always dreaded the result so much that I strove my
hardest to do no more than smile appreciation. My laugh compelled Mrs.
Poppleton to stare at me—oh, her eyes! Thereupon, her husband began
his dread performance. The patience, the heroic patience, of that dear,
good fellow! I have known him explain, and re-explain, for a quarter of
an hour, and invariably without success. It might be a mere pun; Mrs.
Poppleton no more understood the nature of a pun than of the binomial
theorem. But worse was when the jest involved some allusion. When I
heard Poppleton begin to elucidate, to expound, the perspiration
already on his forehead, I looked at him with imploring anguish. Why
 would  he attempt the impossible? But the kind fellow couldn’t
disregard his wife’s request. Shall I ever forget her. “Oh—yes—I
see”?—when obviously she saw nothing but the wall at which she sat
staring.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: A masterpiece of comic narration: Everard's extended anecdote of Poppleton's martyrdom to his wife's stupidity is brilliant, savage, and enormously quotable. The passage exposes Everard's contempt for female incompetence while implicitly indicting marriage itself. It is both darkly comic and thematically central to the novel's exploration of gender, marriage, and male resentment.
enrichment.best_quote: Poor old Poppleton! Again and again I have heard him—what do you think?—laboriously explaining jests to her... I have known him explain, and re-explain, for a quarter of an hour, and invariably without success.
enrichment.summary: Everard elaborates the torture of Poppleton's marriage through extended comic detail: his friend's endless, futile attempts to explain jokes to his wife's blank incomprehension, culminating in the image of her staring unseeing at the wall.

“There, too, I can offer an explanation,” replied Barfoot quietly,
“though you may doubt whether it justifies him. I met Orchard a few
months ago in Alexandria, met him by chance in the street, and didn’t
recognize him until he spoke to me. He was worn to skin and bone. I
found that he had abandoned all his possessions to Mrs. Orchard, and
just kept himself alive on casual work for the magazines, wandering
about the shores of the Mediterranean like an uneasy spirit. He showed
me the thing he had last written, and I see it is published in this
month’s  Macmillan . Do read it. An exquisite description of a night in
Alexandria. One of these days he will starve to death. A pity; he might
have done fine work.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard provides backstory on Orchard's suffering and current wandering life; introduces literary work and foreshadows Everard's philosophy of escape and aesthetic experience.
enrichment.best_quote: He showed me the thing he had last written, and I see it is published in this month's Macmillan. Do read it. An exquisite description of a night in Alexandria.

Miss Barfoot challenges Everard's sympathetic account of Orchard's plight by demanding to know what justification exists for a man deserting his family, prompting Everard to provide a detailed explanation of how Orchard's wife's constant domestic complaints drove him to abandon his marriage.

text:
“Let me give an account of a day I spent with him at Tintern, not long
before I left England. He and his wife were having a holiday there, and
I called on them. We went to walk about the Abbey. Now, for some two
hours—I will be strictly truthful—whilst we were in the midst of that
lovely scenery, Mrs. Orchard discoursed unceasingly of one subject—the
difficulty she had with her domestic servants. Ten or twelve of these
handmaidens were marshalled before our imagination; their names, their
ages, their antecedents, the wages they received, were carefully
specified. We listened to a  catalogue raisonne  of the plates, cups,
and other utensils that they had broken. We heard of the enormities
which in each case led to their dismissal. Orchard tried repeatedly to
change the subject, but only with the effect of irritating his wife.
What could he or I do but patiently give ear? Our walk was ruined, but
there was no help for it. Now, be good enough to extend this kind of
thing over a number of years. Picture Orchard sitting down in his home
to literary work, and liable at any moment to an invasion from Mrs.
Orchard, who comes to tell him, at great length, that the butcher has
charged for a joint they have not consumed—or something of that kind.
He assured me that his choice lay between flight and suicide, and I
firmly believed him.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's second extended anecdote—the Tintern Abbey walk—is brilliantly constructed to justify male desperation. His narrative of Mrs. Orchard's relentless, trivial complaints demonstrates how marriage to an intellectually barren woman constitutes psychological torture. The passage is both entertaining and contains Gissing's implicit argument about female incapacity and marital incompatibility.
enrichment.best_quote: Our walk was ruined, but there was no help for it. Now, be good enough to extend this kind of thing over a number of years... He assured me that his choice lay between flight and suicide, and I firmly believed him.
enrichment.summary: Everard recounts a day when Orchard and he walked at Tintern Abbey while Mrs. Orchard discoursed ceaselessly for two hours about domestic servants and broken crockery, illustrating Orchard's desperate choice between escape and death.

# Context for Chunk Positioning

Everard Barfoot has been invited to dinner at his cousin Miss Barfoot's home. During the meal, he entertains the company with witty anecdotes about mutual acquaintances whose marriages have failed. After dinner, the ladies withdraw to the drawing room while Everard remains to drink wine. Rhoda Nunn then deliberately leaves the drawing room to go to the library, giving Miss Barfoot and Everard privacy for conversation. When Everard joins his cousin in the drawing room, he discovers that Rhoda has strategically absented herself, leaving him alone with Miss Barfoot for their discussion about his future plans and lack of professional ambition.

“He determined that his boys should be gentlemen. Tom, the elder,
followed his wishes exactly; he was remarkably clever, but idleness
spoilt him, and now he has made that ridiculous marriage—the end of
poor Tom. Everard went to Eton, and the school had a remarkable effect
upon him; it made him a furious Radical. Instead of imitating the young
aristocrats he hated and scorned them. There must have been great force
of originality in the boy. Of course I don’t know whether any Etonians
of his time preached Radicalism, but it seems unlikely. I think it was
sheer vigour of character, and the strange desire to oppose his father
in everything. From Eton he was of course to pass to Oxford, but at
that stage came practical rebellion. No, said the boy; he wouldn’t go
to a university, to fill his head with useless learning; he had made up
his mind to be an engineer. This was an astonishment to every one;
engineering didn’t seem at all the thing for him; he had very little
ability in mathematics, and his bent had always been to liberal
studies. But nothing could shake his idea. He had got it into his head
that only some such work as engineering—something of a practical kind,
that called for strength and craftsmanship—was worthy of a man with
his opinions. He would rank with the classes that keep the world going
with their sturdy toil: that was how he spoke. And, after a great
fight, he had his way. He left Eton to study civil engineering.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Extended, fascinating narrative of Everard's youth: his rebellion at Eton, his Radicalism, his deliberate rejection of Oxford for engineering despite unsuitability, his stubborn commitment to work he loathed for years out of refusal to admit error. This passage is central to understanding Everard's character—his force of will, his need to oppose his father, his capacity for self-torture. It is brilliantly narrated and thematically crucial to the novel.
enrichment.best_quote: He would rank with the classes that keep the world going with their sturdy toil: that was how he spoke. And, after a great fight, he had his way. He left Eton to study civil engineering.
enrichment.summary: Mary recounts Everard's Radical rejection of Oxford in favor of engineering, his lack of mathematical ability, and his stubborn commitment to a profession unsuited to him out of sheer will to oppose his father.

soul on Trilinear Co-ordinates. Shall I run down to Sheffield to see
you, or is there any chance of the holidays bringing you this way? I
have found a cheap flat, poorly furnished, in Bayswater; the man who

“I admire your old-fashioned sentiment, Micklethwaite. It sits well on
you, and you’re a fine fellow. But I have much more sympathy with the
new idea that women should think of marriage only as men do—I mean,
not to grow up in the thought that they must marry or be blighted
creatures. My own views are rather extreme, perhaps; strictly, I don’t
believe in marriage at all. And I haven’t anything like the respect for
women, as women, that you have. You belong to the Ruskin school; and
I—well, perhaps my experience has been unusual, though I don’t think
so. You know, by-the-bye, that my relatives consider me a blackguard?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's articulate statement of his radical views on marriage and women is philosophically central to the novel; he contrasts himself with Micklethwaite and hints at a dark past.

“I had an odd thought whilst I was there.” Everard leaned his head
back, and half closed his eyes. “Miss Nunn, I warrant, considers
herself proof against any kind of wooing. She is one of the grandly
severe women; a terror, I imagine, to any young girl at their place who

man of my kind. There would be something piquant in making vigorous
love to Miss Nunn, just to prove her sincerity.”

“I confess to you that women have spoilt me. And I am rather resentful
when any one cries out against me for lack of respect to womanhood. I
have been the victim of this groundless veneration for females. Now you
shall hear the story; and bear in mind that you are the only person to
whom I have ever told it. I never tried to defend myself when I was
vilified on all hands. Probably the attempt would have been useless;
and then it would certainly have increased the odium in which I stood.
I think I’ll tell cousin Mary the truth some day; it would be good for
her.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's extended reflection on his experience with women, his lack of respect for them, his victimization by 'veneration,' and his resolve to finally tell the truth is foundational to his character and the novel's psychology.

“Well now, I was staying in the summer with some friends of ours at a
little place called Upchurch, on a branch line from Oxford. The people
were well-to-do—Goodall their name—and went in for philanthropy. Mrs.
Goodall always had a lot of Upchurch girls about her, educated and not;
her idea was to civilize one class by means of the other, and to give a
new spirit to both. My cousin Mary was staying at the house whilst I
was there. She had more reasonable views than Mrs. Goodall, but took a
great interest in what was going on.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's background exposition on the Goodall family's social experiment and Mary's involvement establishes context for the scandal, showing wealth-based philanthropy.

“It happened that by the very train which took me back to London, when
my visit was over, this girl also travelled, and alone. I saw her at
Upchurch Station, but we didn’t speak, and I got into a smoking

platform, Amy put herself in my way, so that I was obliged to begin
talking with her. This behaviour rather surprised me. I wondered what
Mrs. Goodall would think of it. But perhaps it was a sign of innocent
freedom in the intercourse of men and women. At all events, Amy managed
to get me into the same carriage with herself, and on the way to London
we were alone. You foresee the end of it. At Paddington Station the
girl and I went off together, and she didn’t get to her sister’s till
the evening.

Everard Barfoot recounts to his friend Micklethwaite a controversial incident from his past involving a young woman named Amy Drake. During a train journey from Oxford to London, Barfoot encounters Amy, who deliberately positions herself to travel alone with him in the same carriage. This encounter leads to a compromising situation at Paddington Station that becomes the source of scandal and reputational damage to Barfoot, as he is blamed for seducing an innocent girl, though he later reveals Amy was experienced and deliberately deceived him to create the scandal.

text:
“Of course I take it for granted that you believe my account of the
matter. Miss Drake was by no means the spiritual young person that Mrs.
Goodall thought her, or hoped to make her; plainly, she was a reprobate
of experience. This, you will say, doesn’t alter the fact that I also
behaved like a reprobate. No; from the moralist’s point of view I was
to blame. But I had no moral pretentions, and it was too much to expect
that I should rebuke the young woman and preach her a sermon. You admit
that, I dare say?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's admission that Amy was experienced and his justification that he took no moral responsibility is central to understanding his character and moral framework.
enrichment.best_quote: Of course I take it for granted that you believe my account of the matter. Miss Drake was by no means the spiritual young person that Mrs. Goodall thought her, or hoped to make her; plainly, she was a reprobate of experience.
enrichment.summary: Everard insists Amy was experienced, not innocent, and thus he bore no responsibility for seducing her as she was already a 'reprobate.'

“Amy was not only a reprobate, but a rascal. She betrayed me to the
people at Upchurch, and, I am quite sure, meant from the first to do
so. Imagine the outcry. I had committed a monstrous crime—had led
astray an innocent maiden, had outraged hospitality—and so on. In
Amy’s case there were awkward results. Of course I must marry the girl
forthwith. But of course I was determined to do no such thing. For the
reasons I have explained, I let the storm break upon me. I had been a
fool, to be sure, and couldn’t help myself. No one would have believed
my plea—no one would have allowed that the truth was an excuse. I was
abused on all hands. And when, shortly after, my father made his will
and died, doubtless he cut me off with my small annuity on this very
account. My cousin Mary got a good deal of the money that would
otherwise have been mine. The old man had been on rather better terms
with me just before that; in a will that he destroyed I believe he had
treated me handsomely.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's account of Amy's betrayal, her accusation that he seduced her innocently, the social outcry, and his father's disinheritance reveal the scandal's consequences and his family's judgment of his character.
